title: Atoms: how small they are and what is inside them
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Changes made: the paper strip is now 24 cm long and cut across its width, so there is always a long edge to hold, and a grown-up does the cuts below 1 cm with sharp scissors. The hidden-object marble test now names a smooth floor, card raised on four steel tumblers and a battery standing up, because marbles stop on carpet and a flat coin lets them roll over it. The colour test uses hot water from a kettle, not a hot tap, which many Indian homes do not have, and it gives food colour, ink or instant coffee as choices. The salt-flame test needs a gas stove, so it gives a street-light and video alternative for homes with induction cooktops. The battery in the marble test is pressed into a small ball of chapati dough, so a marble cannot knock it over. Rubbed balloons often fail in humid or monsoon weather, so magnets are the first choice. Parents should know: the smell race is mostly carried by moving air, and the hot colour glass mostly by moving water, not by the molecules wandering alone. The unit says so. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 to 90 minutes. Catch the Electron and the size ladder both work for one child alone.

summary.text: Cut a strip of paper in half again and again, and your scissors stop after about 8 cuts. To get a sliver only one atom wide, you would need about 31. Everything you can touch is made of atoms, and an atom is almost all empty space. At its centre is a tiny, heavy nucleus, made of protons and neutrons. Electrons are found around it, not on tracks but in a cloud of places where they are likely to be.
summary.art: A zoom in five circles: a child's hand on a wooden table, the wood's fibres, a cluster of molecules, one atom drawn as a soft glowing cloud, and a tiny bright dot at its centre.

intro.hook: Take a piece of paper. Tear it in half. Tear one half in half again. Keep going. Can you go on for ever? Or will you reach a piece so small it cannot be cut?
intro.text: More than 2,000 years ago, a thinker in India asked this same question. His name was Kanada. A story says he lived on the grains of rice left behind in fields after the harvest. His name may even mean 'grain-eater'. Kanada taught that everything is made of tiny particles, far too small to see. He called them paramanu. Far away in Greece, a thinker called Democritus had a similar idea. He called them atoms. Neither of them had a microscope. They worked it out by thinking. In this unit you test their idea yourself, with a strip of paper and a pair of scissors.
intro.art: A thinker in simple cotton clothes kneeling in a harvested rice field at sunset, holding a single grain of rice up to his eye.

outcomes: I can say that everything I can touch is made of atoms, far too small to see, even with a magnifying glass.
I can show how small atoms are, by cutting paper in half again and again, and by putting things in order of size.
I can name the parts of an atom: a tiny centre called the nucleus, made of protons and neutrons, and electrons around it.
I can explain that an atom is almost all empty space, and how scientists found out by firing alpha particles at thin gold.
I can explain that electrons are not little balls going round on tracks. Scientists can only say where an electron is likely to be found, so they draw it as a cloud.
I can say that the very small does not behave like the things we see. I can also say that in physics an 'observer' is anything that measures, not only a person.
I can say how we know atoms are real without seeing them, and name things scientists still do not know.

terms.meaning: Anything that has weight and takes up space. Solids, liquids and gases are all matter.
terms.example: A stone, water and the air in a balloon are all matter. A shadow is not.
terms.art: A stone, a glass of water and a blown-up balloon side by side, with a shadow on the ground marked with a question mark.

terms.meaning: A very small piece of matter, too small to see. Atoms and molecules are particles. So are the protons, neutrons and electrons inside atoms.
terms.example: Sugar stirred into water breaks up into particles too small to see. You can still taste them.
terms.art: A spoon of sugar stirred into a glass, with a zoomed circle showing tiny dots spread through the water.

terms.meaning: The tiny particle that everything you can touch is built from. An atom has a nucleus at its centre, with electrons around it. About 5 million atoms in a row would be just 1 millimetre long.
terms.example: Your hand, the floor and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A ruler's 1 millimetre gap, with a zoomed circle showing a long row of tiny glowing atoms squeezed into it.

terms.meaning: A substance whose atoms are all of one kind. Atoms are the same kind when they have the same number of protons. About 90 elements are found in nature.
terms.example: Gold, iron, oxygen and carbon are elements. The graphite in a pencil is made only of carbon atoms.
terms.art: A gold earring, an iron nail, a pencil tip and a puff of air, each with a small label.

terms.meaning: Two or more atoms joined together into one particle.
terms.example: A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
terms.art: One big ball with two smaller balls joined to it at an angle, labelled water.

terms.meaning: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom. Nearly all of an atom's weight is in it.
terms.example: If an atom were as big as a cricket ground, its nucleus would be about the size of a peppercorn on the middle stump.
terms.art: A huge cricket ground seen from above, with a single peppercorn glowing on the middle stump.

terms.meaning: One of the two kinds of particle in the nucleus. A proton has a positive electric charge, shown as plus. The number of protons decides which element an atom is.
terms.example: Every carbon atom has 6 protons. Every gold atom has 79.
terms.art: A small cluster of red balls, labelled protons, with a plus sign on each.

terms.meaning: The other kind of particle in the nucleus. A neutron has no electric charge. It weighs about the same as a proton.
terms.example: A carbon atom usually has 6 neutrons next to its 6 protons.
terms.art: A cluster of red and grey balls packed together, the grey ones labelled neutrons.

terms.meaning: A very light particle with a negative electric charge, shown as minus. Electrons are found around the nucleus. When atoms meet, it is their electrons that push on each other or join the atoms together.
terms.example: When you rub a balloon on dry hair, some electrons move from your hair onto the balloon.
terms.art: A fuzzy cloud around a tiny dot, with the cloud labelled electron.

terms.meaning: An even smaller particle. Each proton and each neutron is made mainly of three quarks.
terms.example: A proton is made of two 'up' quarks and one 'down' quark.
terms.art: A proton opened up like a fruit, showing three small coloured dots inside.

terms.meaning: A property of some particles that makes them attract or repel each other. Attract means pull together. Repel means push apart. A plus and a minus attract. Two pluses, or two minuses, repel.
terms.example: Two balloons rubbed on dry hair both get extra electrons, so they repel each other.
terms.art: Two balloons on threads leaning away from each other, small minus signs on both.

terms.meaning: Space with no matter in it. Most of an atom is empty space. Its nucleus is tiny, and its electrons are tiny too, spread out as a cloud.
terms.example: Nearly all of your body is empty space, because nearly all of every atom is.
terms.art: A child's outline filled with a starry darkness and a few tiny dots.

terms.meaning: A picture that shows where an electron is likely to be found. It is thick where the electron is often found and thin where it is rarely found.
terms.example: Drop 50 pencil dots at a target with your eyes closed. They make a cloud that is thick in the middle.
terms.art: A paper covered in pencil dots, thick around a central bindi and thinning out at the edges.

terms.meaning: The science of the very tiniest things, like atoms, electrons and light. It has rules that are very different from the rules for balls and bicycles.
terms.example: Quantum physics explains why salt sprinkled on a gas flame turns it bright yellow.
terms.art: A gas flame flashing bright yellow as a pinch of salt falls into it.

terms.meaning: Finding out something, such as where a thing is, by letting it bump into something else, like light or a detector.
terms.example: To find an electron, scientists let it hit a screen. The screen makes a tiny flash where it hit.
terms.art: A dark screen with one tiny bright flash on it.

terms.meaning: Anything that measures, such as a detector, a screen or even a single particle of light. It does not have to be a person.
terms.example: A camera chip or a speck of dust can 'observe' an electron by being hit by it.
terms.art: A detector box, a speck of dust and a person's eye, all with the same small flash beside them, showing they all count.

terms.meaning: How likely something is to happen. It is the maths of chance.
terms.example: With two dice, a total of 7 is more likely than a total of 12.
terms.art: Two dice showing 3 and 4, with a big 7 and a small 12 beside them.

terms.meaning: One of the fixed amounts of energy an electron in an atom can have. Electrons can only be on these levels, like standing on the steps of a staircase, never in between.
terms.example: When an electron drops down one step, the atom gives out light of one exact colour.
terms.art: A staircase with a small glowing electron jumping down one step and giving off a yellow spark.

terms.meaning: Particles spreading out by themselves, from where there are many to where there are few.
terms.example: The edges of a drop of food colour in still water slowly turn fuzzy, with nobody stirring it.
terms.art: Three glasses in a row showing a drop of colour slowly spreading through still water.

terms.meaning: A special machine that 'feels' a surface with a needle tip only one atom wide. It can make pictures of single atoms.
terms.example: In 1989, scientists used one to spell the letters IBM with 35 single atoms.
terms.art: A needle tip hovering over a bumpy carpet of atoms, with a picture of the atoms on a computer screen nearby.

terms.meaning: The word used by Kanada, a thinker in ancient India, for the smallest particles that everything is made of.
terms.example: Kanada taught that paramanu join in pairs and threes to build bigger things.
terms.art: An old palm-leaf page with dots drawn in pairs and threes.

explanations.definition: Everything you can touch is made of tiny particles called atoms. About 90 kinds of atom are found in nature, and they join in different ways to make everything.
explanations.description: Look around you. A steel tumbler, a mango, your skin and the air look nothing alike. But zoom in far enough and they are all made of atoms. Different things are made of different kinds of atom, joined in different patterns. It is a bit like the alphabet. Just 26 letters make every word in English. About 90 kinds of atom make a stone, a tree and you.
examples: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms, joined in little groups called molecules.
The grey tip of a pencil is mostly graphite, which is made only of carbon atoms. A diamond is made only of carbon atoms too. The atoms are just arranged differently.
Your body is made mostly of four kinds of atom: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen.
explanations.art: Three small models built from the same few kinds of coloured beads: a little house, a tree and a child.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what everything is made of.

explanations.definition: The smallest atom, hydrogen, is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. Most atoms are two or three times wider. That is still far too small to see with any ordinary microscope.
explanations.description: Small numbers are hard to imagine, so try halving. Take a strip of paper 24 centimetres long and cut it in half. Then cut one half in half. Keep going. With home scissors, most people can make about 8 cuts. The piece is then a sliver about 1 millimetre wide. To make it just one atom wide, you would need about 31 cuts. Even then, the sliver would still be 2 centimetres long and hundreds of thousands of atoms thick. To reach the width of an atom's centre, you would need about 45 cuts. The chart shows how far each thing is down this halving ladder.
examples: About 5 million atoms side by side would fit across the 1 millimetre gap between two lines on a ruler.
A single hair is a few hundred thousand atoms thick.
One grain of salt holds about a million million million atoms.
explanations.art: A strip of paper cut into smaller and smaller pieces, the last ones vanishing into a magnifier that shows a dot labelled 'still 23 cuts to go'.
explanations.context: Remember the paper strip that you cut in half again and again? This card shows how many more cuts it would take to make a piece one atom wide.

chart.title: How many times you would have to halve a 24 cm strip to get down to the size of each thing
chart.note: Worked out with maths, not cut for real. Most people stop at about 8 cuts, when the scissors can't cut any more.

explanations.concept: How we know atoms are real
explanations.definition: We know atoms are real because of what they do. Moving molecules bump tiny specks in water and make them jiggle. Special microscopes can now make pictures of single atoms.
explanations.description: For more than 2,000 years, atoms were only an idea. Some famous scientists, as late as the year 1900, said atoms were just a handy way of thinking. Then came proof. In 1827, Robert Brown saw tiny specks from pollen jiggling in water, never still. In 1905, Albert Einstein showed that invisible water molecules bumping the specks would make exactly that jiggle. In 1908, Jean Perrin in France measured it carefully, and Einstein was right. In 1981, Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer built the scanning tunnelling microscope. Its needle tip feels a surface like a finger reading bumps. At last we could make pictures of single atoms.
examples: The edges of a drop of food colour in still water slowly turn fuzzy. Water molecules keep bumping the colour's molecules.
In 1989, Don Eigler and Erhard Schweizer moved 35 single atoms to spell the letters IBM.
In 2013, IBM scientists made a tiny cartoon film called 'A Boy and His Atom' by moving single molecules.
explanations.art: A bumpy computer picture of single atoms in neat rows, a few arranged to spell three letters.
explanations.context: Nobody has seen an atom with their own eyes. This card explains how scientists became sure atoms are real.

explanations.description: Long before experiments, thinkers in India and in Greece imagined that everything is made of tiny particles. They had no microscopes. They worked it out by thinking and arguing. Who was first is not known for sure.
examples: Kanada called the tiny particles paramanu. Democritus called them atomos, which means 'uncuttable'.
In 1808, John Dalton in England gave the first evidence from chemistry: elements always join in fixed amounts.

perspectives.who: Kanada, founder of the Vaisheshika school of thought in ancient India
perspectives.explanation: Everything is made of paramanu: tiny, invisible particles that last for ever. They join in pairs and threes to build bigger things. Scholars do not know when Kanada lived. Guesses range from about 600 to 200 years before the Common Era.

perspectives.who: Democritus, a thinker in ancient Greece, about 2,400 years ago, with his teacher Leucippus
perspectives.explanation: Everything is made of atoms moving in empty space. Atoms differ in shape and size, and that is why things differ.

Both traditions seem to have had the idea on their own. Claims that one was clearly first go beyond the evidence. Both were brilliant guesses, and both were partly wrong. Atoms can be cut: they have smaller parts inside.

explanations.art: Two old thinkers on opposite sides of a map, one in India and one in Greece, each drawing dots in the sand.
explanations.context: The idea of atoms is very old. This card is about who had it first, which is still argued about.

explanations.concept: What an atom is made of
explanations.definition: An atom has a tiny centre, the nucleus, made of protons and neutrons. Electrons are found around it. Protons and neutrons are made of even smaller particles called quarks.
explanations.description: The number of protons decides what an atom is. One proton makes hydrogen. Six make carbon. Seventy-nine make gold. Protons are positive and electrons are negative, so they attract each other. That attraction keeps the electrons around the nucleus. Neutrons have no charge. As far as anyone knows, electrons and quarks are not made of anything smaller. But nobody can be sure.
examples: J.J. Thomson found the electron in 1897, in England.
James Chadwick found the neutron in 1932.
Quarks were first imagined in 1964 by Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig. Experiments found signs of them in 1968.
explanations.art: A cut-away atom: a fuzzy outer cloud labelled electrons, a tiny centre of red and grey balls, and one ball opened to show three quarks.
explanations.context: An atom is not the smallest thing after all. This card opens one up to show the parts inside.

explanations.concept: An atom is almost all empty space
explanations.definition: Nearly all of an atom is empty space. The nucleus is tens of thousands of times smaller across than the whole atom, yet it holds nearly all the weight.
explanations.description: In 1909, in Manchester in England, Hans Geiger and a 20-year-old student, Ernest Marsden, fired alpha particles at very thin metal foil. Alpha particles are tiny, fast particles shot out by radium, the element found by Marie and Pierre Curie. Almost every alpha particle went straight through the metal. But about 1 in every 8,000 bounced back. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford explained why. Each atom has a tiny, heavy centre with a strong positive charge. The rest is almost empty. Most alpha particles miss the centre. The rare one that comes close is repelled hard and bounces back.
examples: If a room were one atom, its nucleus would be a speck in the middle, about as wide as a hair.
If all the empty space were squeezed out of every person on Earth, all of us together would fit into about one sugar cube.
explanations.art: Arrows flying at a row of atoms: almost all pass straight through the empty space, one hits a tiny bright centre and bounces back.
explanations.context: Remember the marble test, where marbles rolled under a card and a few came back? This card tells the real experiment that showed atoms are mostly empty.

explanations.definition: Things feel solid because the electrons of one thing push away the electrons of another. A quantum rule also stops electrons from crowding into the same place.
explanations.description: If atoms are nearly empty, why doesn't your hand sink into the table? Two reasons. First, all electrons are negative, and two negative charges repel. When your hand comes near the table, its electrons repel the table's electrons very strongly, long before any nuclei meet. Second, quantum physics has a rule, found by Wolfgang Pauli in 1925. Two electrons can never be in exactly the same state. So electrons cannot squeeze together, and atoms keep their size. What you feel as solid is not atoms packed with no gaps. It is electrons repelling electrons.
examples: Hold two magnets with the same ends facing. You feel them push apart before they touch.
Two rubbed balloons on threads lean away from each other. Their extra electrons repel.
explanations.art: A hand resting on a table, with a zoomed circle showing the electron clouds of the hand and table pressing on each other with a thin gap between them.
explanations.context: If atoms are almost all empty space, why can you lean on a wall? This card explains.

explanations.concept: Electrons are found in clouds, not on tracks
explanations.definition: An electron in an atom does not go round the nucleus on a track. Quantum physics can only say how likely it is to be found in each place. Scientists draw this as a cloud: thick where the electron is likely to be, thin where it is not.
explanations.description: Many books draw atoms like tiny solar systems, with electrons going round like planets. That picture came from Niels Bohr in 1913. It was a useful step, but it is not right. In 1926, Erwin Schrödinger found the maths that describes electrons. It does not give a track. It gives a cloud of chances. Each time scientists measure an electron, they find it at one spot. Do this many times, and the spots make a cloud, like your pencil dots around the target. Between measurements, the maths does not say the electron is at any one spot.
examples: Close your eyes and drop pencil dots at a target 50 times. The dots make a cloud, thickest near the target.
The electron cloud of a hydrogen atom is shaped like a fuzzy ball. Other clouds are shaped like dumbbells or rings.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: the old planet-style atom with a red cross, and a soft glowing cloud around a dot with a green tick.
explanations.context: Do electrons go round and round like planets? This card explains the cloud picture that scientists use instead.

explanations.concept: The very small does not behave like the things we see
explanations.definition: Atoms, electrons and light follow the rules of quantum physics. Their energy comes in fixed steps, and they can spread out like waves, even though they are always found as single particles.
explanations.description: A ball can roll at any speed you like. An electron in an atom cannot have any energy it likes. It can only sit on certain energy levels, like the steps of a staircase. When it drops down one step, the atom gives out light of one exact colour. That is why salt sprinkled on a gas flame flashes yellow. Electrons can also spread like ripples on water. In 1989, Akira Tonomura's team in Japan sent electrons one at a time past a very thin wire that split their path in two. Each electron landed as a single dot. But thousands of dots built up a pattern of stripes, the pattern ripples make. Nobody knows how to picture this. Scientists only know the maths works, every time it is tested.
examples: Old orange street lights glow one exact colour of yellow-orange, from sodium atoms.
Fireworks get their colours from different atoms: copper for blue-green, strontium for red.
Your phone's chips and screen were designed using quantum physics.
explanations.art: A dark screen slowly filling with single dots that, together, make neat bright and dark stripes.
explanations.context: Balls and bicycles follow rules we can feel. This card is about the very different rules that tiny things follow.

explanations.definition: To measure something tiny, you must let it bump into something, like light or a detector. The bump changes it. In physics, the 'observer' is whatever does the measuring. It does not need to be a person.
explanations.description: When you look at a cricket ball, light bounces off it into your eyes. The light is far too weak to move the ball. But an electron is so tiny that one particle of light can knock it away. So you cannot find an electron without changing it. Quantum physics goes further. In 1927, Werner Heisenberg showed a rule. Nobody can know exactly where an electron is and exactly how fast it is going, both at the same moment. This is not because our tools are poor. It is how nature works. Some people say quantum physics shows that a person's mind makes the world real. Physics does not show that. A detector, a screen or a speck of dust counts as an observer.
examples: In the Catch the Electron game, a torch beam or a paper ball counts as a measurement, not only a person.
Air molecules bumping an electron count as measuring it. That is one reason big things never look fuzzy.
explanations.art: A tiny electron being knocked aside by a ray of light, next to a cricket ball that the same light does not move.
explanations.context: People often say 'in quantum physics, looking changes things'. This card explains what that really means, and what it does not mean.

explanations.concept: What is the electron doing when nothing measures it?
explanations.description: Everyone agrees on the maths, and on what experiments show. They disagree about what is really going on between measurements. This is one of the biggest open arguments in all of science.
examples: Every experiment gives the same results, whichever idea a scientist believes.
Many scientists simply use the maths and leave the meaning to others, because the maths works either way.

perspectives.who: Niels Bohr and Werner Heisenberg, in the 1920s, and many physicists today
perspectives.explanation: Between measurements, the electron has no exact place at all. Only the chances exist. A measurement gives one result.

perspectives.who: David Bohm, an American physicist, in 1952
perspectives.explanation: The electron always has an exact place. A hidden wave guides it, and we cannot know the place without measuring.

perspectives.who: Hugh Everett, an American physicist, in 1957
perspectives.explanation: Every possible result really happens, each in a different branch of the world. We only see one branch.

perspectives.who: What all of them agree on
perspectives.explanation: A measurement is any bump with the wider world, by a detector, light or air. None of these ideas needs a human mind to make it work.

explanations.art: One electron cloud with three thought bubbles above it: a blank question mark, a dot riding a wave, and a branching tree.
explanations.context: Scientists can predict what electrons do. This card is about what they still argue over: what an electron is like when nothing is measuring it.

explanations.concept: Every electron is exactly the same
explanations.definition: Every electron in the universe is exactly the same as every other electron. The same is true of every proton, and of every neutron. There is no way at all to tell two of them apart.
explanations.description: Two mangoes from the same tree always differ a little, if you look closely enough. Two electrons never do. In 1924, Satyendra Nath Bose, a young teacher at Dacca University, now in Bangladesh, worked out how to count particles of light that are perfectly identical. A journal did not accept his paper. He sent it to Albert Einstein, who translated it and had it published. Einstein then took the idea further. Today a whole family of tiny particles is called bosons, after Bose.
examples: An electron in your fingertip and an electron in a faraway star are exactly alike.
The particles of light are bosons, named after Satyendra Nath Bose.
explanations.art: Two identical glowing dots, one labelled 'in your finger' and one labelled 'in a star', with an equals sign between them.
explanations.context: No two leaves or mangoes are exactly alike. This card is about particles that are perfectly alike, and the Indian scientist who counted them.

explanations.concept: Your atoms are very old, and on loan
explanations.definition: Most of the hydrogen in you was made soon after the Big Bang. Nearly all your other atoms were made inside stars. Atoms last for billions of years and keep moving from one thing to another.
explanations.description: The carbon in your fingernails and the oxygen in your blood were made inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born. In 1957, Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle showed how stars build atoms. Atoms do not wear out. Every breath you take holds more molecules than there are grains of sand on all the world's beaches. Some of those molecules were breathed before by other people and animals, long ago. A grown-up's body is made of about 7 followed by 27 zeros atoms. You are always swapping some of them with the world around you.
examples: The iron in your blood was made inside stars.
The water you drink has fallen as rain many times before.
explanations.art: A child breathing out, the breath curling up into the sky towards a faraway exploding star.
explanations.context: This card follows atoms out into the cosmos and back: where the atoms in your body came from.

explanations.concept: Particles from space pass through you
explanations.definition: Fast particles from space, called cosmic rays, hit the air all the time. They make showers of other particles, and some of these pass right through your body.
explanations.description: These particles are far too small to feel. About one or two pass through your hand every second. Scientists catch their tracks with special detectors. In India, Bibha Chowdhuri and D.M. Bose of the Bose Institute in Calcutta, now Kolkata, carried photographic plates up mountains near Darjeeling. Between 1939 and 1942, the plates recorded tracks of a kind of particle called a meson. They published their work in the journal Nature. Later, a team in England led by Cecil Powell used better plates to find one kind of meson, the pion. Powell won the Nobel Prize in 1950. Today, a star is named Bibha after her.
examples: A cloud chamber, made with very cold dry ice and alcohol, shows thin trails of mist where these particles pass.
Big detectors under mountains count particles that pass through the whole Earth.
explanations.art: A young woman scientist on a misty Darjeeling hillside setting down a wooden box of photographic plates, faint particle tracks drawn in the sky above.
explanations.context: Not all particles stay inside atoms. This card is about particles that rain down from space, and an Indian scientist who caught their tracks.

explanations.description: Nobody knows. As far as anyone can tell, electrons and quarks have no size at all. Many physicists now think particles are not really little balls. They may be ripples in invisible 'fields' that fill all of space, like ripples on a pond. Others wonder if space itself is made of tiny separate pieces. Some think there may be tiny vibrating strings deeper down. This is called string theory. No experiment has tested it yet.
examples: Space that looks empty is never quite empty. It fizzes with tiny flickers of energy, which scientists have measured.
A ripple on a pond is not a thing you can pick up. It is the pond moving.

perspectives.explanation: Particles are ripples in fields. The fields are what the world is really made of.

perspectives.who: String theorists, such as Ashoke Sen, an Indian physicist
perspectives.explanation: Deep down, particles may be tiny vibrating strings. Experiments have not tested this idea yet.
We may never be able to see deeper. Some questions about the very small may stay open.

explanations.art: A pond with ripples spreading, the ripples drawn as tiny glowing dots where they peak.
explanations.context: This card goes to the edge of what anyone knows. Is there a bottom to the very small?

agreed.text: Everything we can touch is made of atoms, and about 90 kinds are found in nature.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have weighed elements joining since John Dalton in 1808. Brownian motion, measured by Jean Perrin in 1908, proved atoms are real. Today special microscopes make pictures of single atoms.

agreed.text: Atoms are tiny: about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across.
agreed.evidence: Perrin worked out their size from jiggling specks. X-rays bouncing off crystals and atom-picturing microscopes give the same answer.

agreed.text: Every atom has a tiny, heavy nucleus, and the rest is almost empty space.
agreed.evidence: In 1909, Geiger and Marsden saw about 1 in 8,000 alpha particles bounce back from thin metal foil. Rutherford explained it in 1911.

agreed.text: Electrons do not move on neat tracks. Quantum physics gives the chances of finding them in each place.
agreed.evidence: Its predictions have been tested millions of times, from the colours of flames to the electron stripe experiments. Every phone chip depends on them being right.

agreed.text: Nearly all the atoms in your body, except most of the hydrogen, were made inside stars.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers see these atoms being made and thrown out by stars today. Margaret Burbidge and her colleagues worked out how, in 1957.

challenging.claim: Atoms are tiny hard balls that cannot be split.
challenging.who: John Dalton in 1808, and the old Greek word 'atomos', which means uncuttable
challenging.for: Elements join in fixed amounts, as if they were made of tiny, unchanging balls. This idea helped chemistry for a hundred years.
challenging.against: In 1897 the electron was found inside atoms. In 1911 the nucleus was found. Atoms have parts, and nuclei can even be split.
challenging.context: This card is about an old picture of the atom, and why it changed.

challenging.claim: Electrons go round the nucleus on tracks, like planets round the Sun.
challenging.who: Niels Bohr's model of 1913, still drawn in many books and logos
challenging.for: It explained the exact colours that hydrogen gives out, and it is easy to draw.
challenging.against: It fails for every atom bigger than hydrogen. Since 1926, the maths of quantum physics has shown that electrons have no tracks, only clouds of chances.
challenging.context: This card is about the famous 'solar system' picture of the atom.

challenging.claim: Atoms are not real. They are just a handy way of thinking.
challenging.who: Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, two famous scientists, around 1900
challenging.for: In 1900 nobody had seen an atom, and good science should rest on what can be measured.
challenging.against: Einstein's work on Brownian motion in 1905 and Perrin's measurements in 1908 showed atoms are real. Ostwald changed his mind. Today we picture single atoms.
challenging.context: Around the year 1900, some top scientists doubted atoms existed. This card is about that argument.

challenging.claim: Quantum physics proves that our minds create the world.
challenging.who: Some films, books and speakers, and some people who sell healing or success courses
challenging.for: In quantum physics, measuring does change what you find. And the word 'observer' sounds like it means a person.
challenging.against: In physics, an observer is anything that measures, such as a detector or a particle of light. The experiments work the same with no person watching. Physicists still argue about what measurement means, but none of the main ideas need a person watching.
challenging.context: You may hear people say that quantum physics is about the power of the mind. This card checks that claim.

challenging.claim: Kanada discovered the atom long before anyone else.
challenging.who: Some books and speakers in India
challenging.for: Kanada really did teach that everything is made of tiny invisible particles, paramanu, that join to make bigger things. It was a deep and careful idea.
challenging.against: Nobody knows when Kanada lived. Democritus in Greece had a similar idea about 2,400 years ago. Neither tested it with experiments. Proof came only in the 1900s.
challenging.context: This card is about the credit for the first idea of atoms.

challenging.who: A popular saying in science books and videos
challenging.for: When your hand meets a table, the electrons push each other away before the atoms' centres come anywhere near each other. There is always a tiny gap.
challenging.against: That electric push is what touching is. There is no other kind of touching to compare it with. So in the everyday meaning of the word, you do touch.
challenging.context: This card looks at a famous saying about atoms and asks whether it is fair.

challenging.claim: The dust you see dancing in a sunbeam is being jiggled by atoms.
challenging.who: The Roman poet Lucretius, about 2,000 years ago, and many people since
challenging.for: Atoms really do bump tiny specks and make them jiggle. This is called Brownian motion.
challenging.against: The dust you can see is too big. It swirls mainly because of small air currents. True Brownian motion shows only for much tinier specks, under a microscope.
challenging.context: This card is about a beautiful old example that turned out to be mostly wrong, even though the idea behind it was right.

big_questions.q: If you had perfect scissors and perfect eyes, could you cut a piece of paper in half for ever?
big_questions.hint: The paper is made of atoms. What happens when you reach one? And what is inside it?

big_questions.q: If atoms are almost all empty space, why can't you walk through a wall?
big_questions.hint: Think of two magnets with the same ends facing. Do they need to touch to push?

big_questions.q: Can we know something is real if we can never see it?
big_questions.hint: Nobody saw an atom for 2,000 years. How did scientists become sure? What else do you believe in without seeing it?

big_questions.q: An electron is found in one spot each time we look. Where is it when nothing is looking?
big_questions.hint: Scientists still argue about this. What do you think?

big_questions.q: Your atoms were made in stars and will go on after you. So what is 'you'? The atoms, or the pattern they make?
big_questions.hint: Your atoms keep changing as you eat, breathe and grow. Are you still the same you as last year?

big_questions.q: Kanada and Democritus had the same idea in two faraway places. Does an idea belong to one people, or to everyone?
big_questions.hint: Who should get the credit when two people think of the same thing?

big_questions.q: Ernest Marsden counted flashes in the dark for hours, but Rutherford's name went on the discovery. Who really discovered the nucleus?
big_questions.hint: Geiger and Marsden did the counting. Rutherford worked out what it meant. Can a discovery belong to one person?

big_questions.q: Every electron is exactly the same as every other one. Is anything else in the world exactly the same as something else?
big_questions.hint: Think of two coins, two leaves, two twins. Are they exactly the same?

big_questions.q: If big things are made of tiny things that follow rules of chance, why do big things seem so sure and solid?
big_questions.hint: One dice roll is a surprise. What about the total of a million rolls?
An atom is mostly empty space. But scientists say even empty space fizzes with energy.

big_questions.q: Is there a smallest thing in the world, or does it go on getting smaller for ever?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows. Which do you think is stranger?

story.title: Counting in the Dark
story.note: Real: Ernest Marsden was 20 and a student in Manchester in 1909. He and Hans Geiger counted tiny flashes made by alpha particles from radium, in a darkened room, through a microscope. They found that a few bounced back from metal foil, about 1 in 8,000 for platinum. Rutherford explained it in 1911 with the tiny nucleus. Rutherford's words about the shell and the tissue paper are from a lecture he gave much later. Marsden later moved to New Zealand. Imagined: Marsden's thoughts, the rain, the exact words of the conversations, and the last scene of Marsden in his old age.
text: In the spring of 1909, in the city of Manchester in England, a young man sat alone in a dark room and waited for his eyes to change. His name was Ernest Marsden. He was twenty years old, still a student, and he was fairly sure he had been given the most boring job in the building.

The job came from Professor Ernest Rutherford, a big, loud man from New Zealand, whose laugh shook the windows. Rutherford studied the tiniest things there are. In his laboratory he kept a little tube of radium, the strange element that Marie and Pierre Curie had discovered. Radium shoots out tiny particles, far too small to see. Rutherford called them alpha particles. They fly thousands of times faster than a bullet.

You cannot see an alpha particle. But if one hits a screen coated with a special powder, the powder gives one tiny flash of green light, gone in a moment, like a firefly very far away. To see the flashes, you must first sit in the dark until your eyes are ready. Then you look through a microscope at the screen, and you count.

Marsden's job was to fire alpha particles at a sheet of gold, beaten so thin that light shone through it, soft and green. Hans Geiger, Rutherford's patient German assistant, had shown him how. Almost every alpha particle went straight through the gold, as if it were not there. A few were nudged a little to one side. That was what everyone expected. In those days, scientists pictured an atom as a soft ball of positive charge, with electrons dotted through it like raisins in a pudding. A pudding cannot stop a bullet.
'Now,' Rutherford had said, rubbing his big hands together, 'put your screen on the same side as the radium. See if any of them bounce back.'
'Almost certainly not,' said Rutherford cheerfully. 'But look anyway.'

So Marsden looked. He sat in the dark, and waited for his eyes, and looked, and saw nothing. He rubbed his eyes and looked again. Nothing. Outside, the rain drummed on the roof. He could hear other students laughing in the corridor, on their way to tea. He thought, not for the first time, that this was the job you gave to the youngest person in the building, the one who did not matter.

His eyes ached. The dark seemed to press on them. Once, he almost got up to tell Rutherford that there was nothing to see. But Rutherford had said 'look anyway'. And Marsden was the kind of person who, when he was asked to do something properly, did it properly. So he made himself sit still and keep watching the dark patch of screen, where nothing was supposed to happen.
A flash. One tiny green spark, on the wrong side.
Marsden held his breath. Tired eyes play tricks, he told himself. He waited. The minutes crawled. Another flash. Then, a long time later, another. They were rare, very rare. But they were there.

For days, Marsden and Geiger counted. They tried gold, then platinum and other metals. They counted until their eyes swam with green ghosts. Nearly all the alpha particles went straight through the metal. But about one in every eight thousand came flying back, as if it had hit a wall.

Marsden went to Rutherford and told him. Rutherford did not laugh. He went very quiet. Years later he said it was the most incredible thing that had ever happened to him. It was as if you fired a giant cannon shell at a sheet of tissue paper, and it came back and hit you.

Rutherford thought about it for almost two years. Then he understood. If nearly all the alpha particles went straight through, the gold must be nearly all empty space. If a few bounced back hard, there must be something hiding in that emptiness. Something tiny and heavy, with a strong positive charge, at the very centre of every atom. He called it the nucleus. Each gold atom was not a pudding at all. It was a vast, empty space, with a speck in the middle and its electrons spread thinly around it. If the atom were a cricket ground, the speck would be a peppercorn on the middle stump. Most alpha particles simply flew past the speck. Only the rare one that came very close was thrown back.

The idea became famous, and it was named after Rutherford. Marsden grew older, crossed the world to New Zealand, and became a scientist there. Few people remember the student who sat in the dark and kept looking at the place where nothing was supposed to happen.

But on rainy evenings, in his old age, Marsden would sometimes sit in a dark room on purpose, just for a moment. He would put his hand flat on a table and press. The table pressed back, firm and solid, as tables do. And he would smile, because he knew what the table really was. Almost all empty space, with a tiny speck in the middle of every atom, and electrons pushing back.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story turns on the idea that atoms are almost entirely empty space. Most alpha particles pass straight through the gold because there is almost nothing there to hit. The rare ones that bounce back have met the tiny, heavy nucleus. What feels solid is not atoms packed with no gaps. It is electrons repelling electrons. The story also asks who gets the credit, and why patience in the 'boring' places matters. The last scene with the table is imagined.
ask: Why did Rutherford think no alpha particles would bounce back?
Most alpha particles went straight through the gold. What did that tell Rutherford about atoms?
A few came flying back. What did that tell him?
Why do you think Marsden kept looking, when he thought there was nothing to see?
The idea was named after Rutherford. Do you think Marsden and Geiger should share the credit? Why?

Rutherford, big and cheerful, rubbing his hands together beside a table of glass tubes.

A drawing of arrows flying through a sheet of gold atoms, one arrow bouncing back off a tiny bright speck.

games.title: Smaller and Smaller: the size ladder
games.context: This is a card game about size. Each card shows something real, from the Sun down to an electron. You put them in order, from biggest to smallest, and find out just how small atoms are.

printables.title: 22 size cards to cut out. The front shows a picture and a name. The back shows the size and a number for checking.
items: 1. The Sun: about 1.4 million kilometres across
3. India, from north to south: about 3,200 kilometres
5. A cricket pitch: about 20 metres long
6. An Indian elephant: about 3 metres tall
7. You: about 1 and a quarter metres tall
8. A cricket bat: just under 1 metre long
12. A mustard seed: about 1 millimetre across
13. A grain of salt: about one third of a millimetre
14. The width of a hair: about one tenth of a millimetre
15. A red blood cell: a little less than one hundredth of a millimetre
16. A bacterium: about 2 thousandths of a millimetre
17. A virus: about one ten-thousandth of a millimetre
18. A water molecule: about 3 ten-millionths of a millimetre
19. A hydrogen atom: about one ten-millionth of a millimetre
20. The nucleus of a carbon atom: tens of thousands of times smaller than its atom
21. A proton: smaller still, about a third of a carbon nucleus
22. An electron: nobody has found any size at all. It may have none.

rules: Cut out the 22 cards. Each card has a picture on the front, and its size and a number on the back.

Playing alone: shuffle the cards and take 8. Lay them in a line, biggest on the left and smallest on the right, picture side up. Time yourself. Then turn them over. The numbers should go up from left to right. Each card in the wrong place adds 10 seconds. Try to beat your best time, then try with all 22 cards.
Playing with others: deal 5 cards each, picture side up, and put one card in the middle to start a ladder.
On your turn, put one of your cards into the ladder where you think it belongs. Say why. Someone turns it over to check the number.
If you are right, it stays. If you are wrong, take it back and take one more card from the pile.
The first player with no cards left wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 22 cards. 2. Show your child the front and back of one card. 3. Put the elephant card and the ant card side by side.
flow.say: Each card is something real. Your job is to put them in order of size, biggest to smallest. Which is bigger, the elephant or the ant?
flow.kid: Each card is something real. Put them in order of size. Biggest first, smallest last. Which is bigger, the elephant or the ant?
flow.context: This is the first step of Smaller and Smaller. It is a card game about putting real things in order of size, from the Sun down to an electron.

flow.do: Play a practice round with three cards: the coin, the mustard seed and the hydrogen atom.
flow.say: Let's practise with three cards. Put the coin, the mustard seed and the atom in order, biggest first.
flow.kid: Practice round! Put the coin, the mustard seed and the atom in order. Biggest first.

check.why: A hydrogen atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. A mustard seed is about 1 millimetre. So about 10 million atoms would fit across one mustard seed. Picking the mustard seed usually means thinking that the smallest thing we can see is the smallest thing there is.

flow.do: 1. Play the game, alone or together, using the rules. 2. Each time a card goes in, ask how many times smaller it is than the card before.
flow.say: Put your card where it belongs and tell us why. Then we'll turn it over and check.
flow.kid: Put your card in the ladder. Say why it goes there. Turn it over to check the number. Were you right?

ask.q: Which two cards were hardest to put in order? Why?
good: The salt and the hair, because both are tiny.
The atom and the water molecule, because I can't see either.

flow.parent: Children often get stuck below the hair card, because nothing there can be seen. That is the point of the game. The jump from a virus to an atom is about a thousand times. The jump from an atom to its nucleus is tens of thousands of times.

flow.do: Lay out all 22 cards in the right order. Look at the last three cards together.
flow.say: Look at the end of the ladder. Scientists have found no size at all for an electron. What could it mean to have no size?
flow.kid: Look at the last card. An electron has no size that anyone has found. What do you think that means?
flow.think: Is there a smallest thing in the world? Or does it go on for ever?

check.q: What does the electron card say about its size?
options: It is about the size of a grain of salt
Nobody has found any size at all
It is bigger than an atom
check.why: Experiments have looked very hard. No size has ever been found for an electron. It may be a point, or a ripple, or something we have no word for yet. Picking 'bigger than an atom' usually means thinking of electrons as balls going round outside the atom. Electrons are part of the atom, and far smaller.

games.title: Catch the Electron
games.context: This is a dice game about electrons. An electron is not a little ball on a track. You can never say exactly where it will be found, only how likely each place is. In this game, every roll is one measurement, and the dots you place slowly build an electron cloud.

printables.title: The atom map: a dot in the middle (the nucleus) and three rings of numbered spots
40 small counters: dried tamarind seeds or chana work well
Guess sheet
items: My guess: inner, middle or outer ring

rules: Put the atom map flat on the floor. You need two dice and a bowl of dried tamarind seeds or chana.
The electron is hidden. Nobody knows where it is until it is measured.
Before each roll, every player guesses where the electron will be found: the inner ring, the middle ring or the outer ring. Write your guess down.
Then 'measure' the electron: roll both dice and add them up. Put one bean on the spot with that number. That is where the electron was found this time.
Everyone who guessed the right ring scores one point.
Play 20 rolls. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to score 9 points or more. Bring a torch for the bonus round.
At the end, look at the beans. They make a picture of the electron cloud.

Bonus round with friends: one player holds a torch and is the detector. The others creep towards the nucleus while the torch is off. Anyone the beam lands on is 'measured' and must freeze in that one spot. A rolled paper ball that touches you counts as a measurement too.

flow.do: 1. Put the atom map on the floor. 2. Put a bowl of beans and two dice beside it. 3. Show the nucleus in the middle and the three rings.
flow.say: This map is an atom. The dot in the middle is the nucleus. Somewhere around it is an electron. We can never know exactly where it will be. We can only measure it and see.
flow.kid: This map is an atom. The middle dot is the nucleus. An electron is somewhere around it. Nobody knows where until we measure.
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch the Electron. It is a dice game where each roll is one measurement of an electron, and the beans build up an electron cloud.

flow.do: 1. Before each roll, everyone guesses a ring and writes it down. 2. Roll two dice and add them. 3. Put a bean on that number's spot. 4. Score a point for each right guess. 5. Play 20 rolls.
flow.say: Guess first: inner, middle or outer ring? Now let's measure. Roll the dice, add them, and put a bean where the electron was found.
flow.kid: Guess a ring. Roll both dice and add them. Put a bean on that number. Did you guess right?

ask.q: Which ring is the best one to guess? Why?
good: The inner ring, because 6, 7 and 8 come up a lot.
The inner ring, because there are more ways to make 7 than 12.

flow.parent: With two dice, 6, 7 and 8 come up most often, about 4 rolls in every 9. A child who always guesses the inner ring will usually win. That is the lesson: you can know the chances, but never the next result. This is how quantum physics treats electrons.

flow.do: Look at the beans on the map together after 20 rolls.
flow.say: Look at the beans. Where are they thickest? This is how scientists draw an electron. They call it an electron cloud.
flow.kid: Look at your beans. Where are there lots? Where are there few? You made an electron cloud!

check.q: After 20 measurements, what do the beans show?
options: Exactly where the electron will be next time
Where the electron is likely to be found: a cloud, thick near the middle
The track the electron goes round on
check.why: Each bean is one measurement. Together they show where the electron is likely and unlikely to be. They cannot tell you the next spot. Picking 'the track' usually comes from the old planet picture of the atom. Real electrons have no track, only a cloud of chances.

flow.do: Play the torch bonus round if you have friends. Then talk about who or what can measure.
flow.say: In the torch round, the torch was the detector. And the paper ball measured you too. Does a measurement need a person?
flow.kid: Did you need a person to measure you? Or could a torch beam or a paper ball do it?
flow.parent: Say clearly: in physics, an 'observer' is anything that measures. A detector, a beam of light or even air molecules can measure an electron. No person needs to watch. Some people claim quantum physics proves our minds make the world. It does not.
flow.think: If a speck of dust can 'measure' an electron, what does the word observer really mean?
