items.p: What is everything around you made of, deep down?
opts: Only the things you can see
items.why: Everything, from stones to air to you, is made of atoms. Picking 'only the things you can see' is a natural idea, because atoms are far too small to see. Picking 'air' misses that air is itself made of atoms.
items.art: A stone, a leaf and a child, each with a zoomed circle of tiny dots.

items.p: You can see a single atom with an ordinary magnifying glass.
items.why: False. An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. A magnifying glass makes things only a few times bigger. Even a strong school microscope cannot show single atoms.

items.p: The tiny particles that everything you can touch is made of are called ____.
items.why: Atoms are the building blocks of all matter.

items.p: You cut a 24 cm strip of paper in half. How long is one piece?
items.why: Half of 24 is 12, because 12 + 12 = 24. Picking 48 usually means doubling instead of halving. Picking 6 means cutting twice.
items.context: This question is about the paper-cutting experiment. You cut a 24 cm strip of paper in half, then cut one half in half, again and again.

items.p: In the paper-cutting experiment, why did you have to stop after about 8 cuts?
opts: The piece got too small to hold and cut with scissors
We had reached a single atom
Paper cannot be cut any more after 8 cuts
items.why: The piece was about 1 millimetre long, too small for fingers and scissors. You were still about 23 cuts away from a piece one atom wide. Picking 'we reached an atom' is very common. The last piece still had millions of atoms across it.
items.context: This question is about the paper-cutting experiment. You cut a 24 cm strip of paper in half, then cut one half in half, again and again.

items.p: Put these in order, from BIGGEST to SMALLEST: an atom, an ant, a grain of salt, an elephant.
items.why: An elephant is about 3 metres tall, an ant about 4 millimetres, a grain of salt about a third of a millimetre. An atom is millions of times smaller than the salt grain.

items.p: Match each part of an atom to what it is.
pairs: in the centre, with a plus charge
in the centre, with no charge
found around the centre, with a minus charge
items.why: Protons and neutrons are packed in the nucleus. Electrons are found in a cloud around it.
items.context: An atom has a tiny, heavy centre called the nucleus, made of protons and neutrons. Electrons are found around it.

items.p: Where is nearly all of an atom's weight?
opts: In the tiny centre, the nucleus
items.why: Protons and neutrons are about 1,800 times heavier than electrons, and they are all in the nucleus. Picking 'in the electrons' often comes from pictures where electrons are drawn big. They are actually very light.

items.p: An atom is almost all empty space.
items.why: True. The nucleus is tens of thousands of times smaller across than the atom. The electrons are tiny too, spread out as a cloud. So almost all of the atom is empty space.

items.p: If an atom were as big as a cricket ground, how big would its nucleus be?
opts: About as big as a peppercorn
About as big as a cricket ball
As big as the whole ground
items.why: The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom, like a peppercorn on the middle stump. Picking 'a cricket ball' is a very common guess. Even that is far too big. It shows how hard it is to imagine how empty atoms are.

items.p: Scientists draw an electron as a cloud. What does the cloud show?
opts: Where the electron is likely to be found
That electrons are soft and fluffy like cotton
Smoke coming out of the atom
items.why: The cloud is a picture of chances: thick where the electron is often found, thin where it is rarely found. Picking 'soft and fluffy' takes the picture too literally. An electron is not made of fluff.

items.p: Electrons go round the centre of an atom on neat tracks, like planets round the Sun.
items.why: False. That picture was drawn in 1913 and is still in many books. But quantum physics shows electrons have no tracks. We can only say where they are likely to be.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one made of atoms, or not made of atoms?
items.why: Air, gold, breath and smells are matter, so they are made of atoms. A smell is tiny molecules reaching your nose. A shadow is just a place where light is blocked. Sunlight is light, which is not made of atoms.

items.p: In physics, what is an 'observer'?
opts: Anything that measures, like a detector, a screen or even light
Only a person who is watching
items.why: In physics, an observer is anything that measures, so anything that a particle bumps into. Picking 'only a person' is the most common mix-up. Experiments work the same way with no person watching.

items.p: Your friend says, 'Air is nothing.' What would you tell them? Give one way to prove it.
items.a: Air is made of tiny particles called molecules, too small to see. One proof: push a dry tissue into a glass, turn it upside down and push it into water. The tissue stays dry, because air fills the glass.
items.why: Any correct test that shows air takes up space, pushes or carries smells is a good answer.

items.p: Draw an atom the honest way. Put a tiny dot for the nucleus in the middle, and a cloud for the electrons around it. Label both.
items.a: A very small dot in the middle labelled nucleus, with a soft, dotty cloud around it labelled electron cloud, thicker near the middle.
items.why: The nucleus is tiny and in the middle. Electrons are drawn as a cloud, not as balls on rings.
items.art: An empty square with a tiny dot in the middle.

items.p: In the marble test, a single battery was hidden under the card. Most of the marbles went straight through. Why?
opts: The battery was small, and most of the space under the card was empty
The marbles were too fast to stop
items.why: Most marbles missed the small battery, because most of the space was empty. The same thing happened with gold atoms in 1909. Picking 'too fast to stop' misses why a few did come back: they hit the battery.
items.context: This question is about the marble test. You hide something under a card held up on four tumblers, then roll marbles under it and watch where they come out.

chart.title: Made-up example: what happened to 20 marbles when one battery was hidden

items.p: In 1909, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at thin metal. What surprised everyone?
items.why: Everyone expected them all to go through, because atoms were pictured as soft puddings. About 1 in 8,000 bounced back. So each atom must have a tiny, heavy centre. Picking 'they all went straight through' is what scientists expected, but not what they saw.

items.p: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom is called the ____.
items.why: Ernest Rutherford named it in 1911. It holds the protons and neutrons.

items.p: In the colour test, which glass did the colour spread through faster, and why?
opts: The hot one, because hot water moves more
The cold one, because cold water is heavier
Both the same, because it is the same colour
Neither, colour only spreads if you stir
items.why: Hot water stirs itself: warm water rises and cooler water sinks. Its molecules also move faster. Picking 'only if you stir' is a common idea, but the test shows the colour spreads with nobody stirring.
items.context: This question is about the colour test. You put one drop of food colour into a glass of hot water and a glass of cold water, without stirring.

items.p: In the colour test, the colour spread in the cold glass too, even though nobody stirred it.
items.why: True. It spread more slowly, but it still spread. Water is never perfectly still, and its molecules are always moving, even in cold water.
items.context: This question is about the colour test. You put one drop of food colour into a glass of hot water and a glass of cold water, without stirring.

items.p: A grown-up squeezes an orange peel at one end of a room. Soon you smell it at the other end. What reached your nose?
opts: Molecules from the orange, too small to see
Nothing, a smell is just an idea
items.why: Molecules float off the orange and the air carries them to your nose. Picking 'nothing' is a common idea, because smells are invisible. But you can only smell something when its molecules arrive.
items.context: This question is about the Smell Race, where everyone stands still in a room and waits to smell an orange peel.

items.p: In the pencil-dot activity, where did most dots land?
opts: Near the target, and fewer further away
items.why: Most dots land near the target, and they thin out further away. That makes a cloud, like the picture of an electron. Picking 'all on the target' would need perfect aim with your eyes closed.
items.context: This question is about the pencil-dot activity. You close your eyes and try to dot a target 50 times, then count the dots in rings around it.

chart.title: Made-up example: where 50 pencil dots landed
chart.note: The inner ring is also the smallest ring. So the dots are packed most tightly near the target.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: saw alpha particles bounce back from metal foil
items.why: Over 35 years, these scientists opened up the atom, one part at a time.
items.context: This question is about the scientists who found the parts of the atom.

items.p: If atoms are almost all empty space, why does a table feel solid?
opts: The electrons in your hand and the table push each other away
The atoms are packed with no gaps
Gravity pushes up from the table
items.why: Electrons all have a minus charge, so they push each other away. A quantum rule also stops them squeezing together. Picking 'no gaps' is the old idea of atoms as hard balls.

items.p: A grown-up sprinkles salt on a gas flame and it flashes yellow. Why?
opts: Electrons in sodium atoms drop down an energy step and give out yellow light
items.why: Heat lifts electrons up an energy step, and when they drop back each gives out light of one exact colour. Picking 'salt burns' is a sensible guess, but the salt is not burning. Its atoms are glowing.
items.context: This question is about the salt-flame activity, where a grown-up sprinkles a pinch of salt on a gas flame.

items.p: An electron in an atom can only have certain amounts of energy, like standing on the steps of a staircase, never in between.
items.why: True. These steps are called energy levels. It is one of the ways the very small does not behave like a ball rolling down a ramp, which can stop anywhere.
items.context: This question is about the staircase game, where you act as an electron jumping up and down steps.

items.p: Put these in order, from BIGGEST to SMALLEST: a proton, an atom, a quark, a nucleus.
items.why: The nucleus is inside the atom, protons are inside the nucleus, and quarks are inside protons. Nobody has measured any size for a quark at all.
items.context: An atom has a tiny, heavy centre called the nucleus, made of protons and neutrons. Electrons are found around it.

items.p: The word 'atom' comes from an old Greek word. What does it mean?
items.why: Democritus thought atoms could not be cut. We now know they can be split into smaller parts. Picking 'tiny' is a good guess, because atoms are tiny, but the word was about cutting.

items.p: Kanada in India and Democritus in Greece both thought everything is made of tiny particles. Neither had a microscope. How might they have come up with the idea?
items.a: For example: they might have noticed that sugar disappears in water but can still be tasted, or that stone steps wear away bit by bit. They thought about cutting things smaller and smaller, and decided there must be a smallest piece.
items.why: Any answer that uses everyday clues and careful thinking is good. They worked by reasoning, not by experiments.
items.context: Kanada was a thinker in ancient India, and Democritus a thinker in ancient Greece. Both lived more than 2,000 years ago.

items.p: Finish the marble test like a scientist. Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
items.a: What I think: the small hidden thing took up only a tiny part of the space under the card. What I saw: with the battery, 18 of 20 marbles went straight through and only 1 came back. Why: most marbles missed it, because most of the space was empty, like a gold atom.
items.why: A good answer has all three parts: a claim, evidence with numbers, and a reason.
items.context: This question is about the marble test. You hide something under a card held up on four tumblers, then roll marbles under it and watch where they come out.

items.p: Draw the card from the marble test, seen from above. Draw the battery as a dot. Draw arrows for 6 marbles: 5 going straight through and 1 bouncing back off the battery.
items.a: A square with a small dot. Five straight arrows crossing it without touching the dot. One arrow hitting the dot and turning back.
items.why: This is just what Rutherford pictured for alpha particles passing through gold atoms.
items.context: This question is about the marble test. You hide something under a card held up on four tumblers, then roll marbles under it and watch where they come out.
items.art: An empty square outline seen from above.

items.p: About how many times would you have to halve a 24 cm strip to get a sliver only one atom wide?
items.why: Each halving makes the piece half as long. After about 31 halvings, the piece would be only about one atom wide. Picking 8 means the scissors' stopping point was taken for an atom. Picking a million forgets how fast halving shrinks things: each cut halves everything that is left.
items.context: This question is about the paper-cutting experiment. You cut a 24 cm strip of paper in half, then cut one half in half, again and again.

answer_chart.title: How many times you would have to halve a 24 cm strip to get down to the size of each thing
answer_chart.note: Worked out with maths, not cut for real. Most people stop at about 8 cuts, when the scissors can't cut any more.

items.p: Some people say quantum physics proves that our minds create the world. What do physicists say?
opts: No. In physics, an observer is anything that measures, and experiments work with no person watching.
Yes. Nothing exists unless a person looks at it.
Yes, but only for big things like tables
items.why: A detector, a screen or air molecules all count as measuring. Experiments give the same results whether or not a person is in the room. Picking 'nothing exists unless a person looks' comes from mixing up the physics word 'observer' with its everyday meaning.

items.p: Every electron is exactly the same as every other electron, everywhere in the universe.
items.why: True. There is no way at all to tell two electrons apart. Satyendra Nath Bose's work in 1924 used this kind of perfect sameness to count particles of light.

items.p: If all the empty space were squeezed out of the atoms of every person on Earth, how big would all of humanity be?
opts: About the size of a sugar cube
About the size of a house
items.why: Nearly all of an atom is empty, and nearly all its weight is in the tiny nucleus. Squeeze out the emptiness, and the whole human race would fit in a sugar cube. It would still weigh about 500 million tonnes. Picking 'a house' is already a huge squeeze, but not nearly enough.

items.p: How do scientists make pictures of single atoms today?
opts: A super-sharp needle tip feels the surface, bump by bump
items.why: The scanning tunnelling microscope, built in 1981 by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, feels a surface with a tip only one atom wide. Picking 'a very strong magnifying glass' is natural, but light waves are thousands of times longer than an atom is wide, so they cannot show single atoms.

items.p: Protons and neutrons are each made mainly of three even smaller particles called ____.
items.why: Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig imagined quarks in 1964. Experiments found signs of them in 1968.

items.p: Why can nobody know exactly where an electron is and exactly how fast it is going, at the same moment?
opts: It is a rule of nature in quantum physics, not just a problem with our tools
Our tools are not good enough yet, and better tools will fix it
Electrons move too fast to film
items.why: Werner Heisenberg showed this in 1927. Measuring always means bumping, but the rule goes deeper than that: an electron does not have an exact place and an exact speed together. Picking 'better tools will fix it' is the most common idea. Physicists have tested this, and it is part of how nature works.

items.p: What is an electron doing between measurements, when nothing is bumping it?
opts: It disappears and is made again
items.why: Physicists agree on the maths and on the results of every experiment. They disagree about what is really happening in between. Picking 'going round on a track' is the old planet picture, which experiments have ruled out.

items.p: Match each scientist to their idea about electrons between measurements.
pairs: it has no exact place until it is measured
it always has an exact place, guided by a hidden wave
every possible result happens, in different branches
items.why: These are three of the main ideas. None of them needs a human mind to do the measuring.
items.context: Physicists agree on what experiments show, but argue about what an electron is like when nothing measures it.

items.p: Nearly all the atoms in your body, apart from most of the hydrogen, were made inside stars.
items.why: True. Hydrogen was made soon after the Big Bang. Heavier atoms, like the carbon in your nails and the iron in your blood, were made in stars. Margaret Burbidge and her colleagues showed how in 1957.

items.p: Bibha Chowdhuri and D.M. Bose caught tracks of tiny particles from space on photographic plates. Where did they take their plates?
items.why: High mountains get more of these particles, because there is less air above to stop them. Their work, from 1939 to 1942, was an early step in finding mesons. Picking 'the Moon' is fun, but nobody went there until 1969.
items.context: Cosmic rays are fast particles from space that hit the air and make showers of other particles.

items.p: A book says, 'You never really touch anything, because atoms push each other away before they meet.' Do you agree? Give a reason for each side.
items.a: For example: in one way it is true, because the electrons push apart and the centres of the atoms never meet. But that push is what we mean by touching. So in another way, we do touch.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason for each side.

items.p: The space inside an atom is called empty. Is it truly empty? What do you think?
items.a: For example: it has no atoms in it, so in that way it is empty. But the electron cloud spreads through it, and scientists say even empty space fizzes with tiny flickers of energy. So perhaps nothing is truly empty.
items.why: Any thoughtful answer is good. Scientists themselves say empty space is never perfectly empty.

items.p: Why can't we say for sure whether Kanada or Democritus had the idea of atoms first?
opts: Nobody knows when Kanada lived. Scholars guess between about 600 and 200 years before the Common Era.
items.why: Democritus lived about 2,400 years ago, and his dates are fairly well known. Kanada's dates are not. So who was first is uncertain. Picking 'they had microscopes' misses that both worked only by thinking.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether colour spreads faster in hot water than in cold water. What will you keep the same?
items.a: Use two glasses of the same size with the same amount of water. Wait until both are still. Add one drop to each at the same moment. Don't stir. Keep everything the same except how warm the water is.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing, here the warmth of the water, and keeps everything else the same.
items.context: This question is about the colour test. You put one drop of food colour into a glass of hot water and a glass of cold water, without stirring.

items.p: Draw a zoom in 6 circles: your hand, your skin, one cell, one molecule, one atom, and the atom's nucleus. Label each circle.
items.a: Six circles, each a closer zoom: a hand, skin, a cell, a molecule of joined balls, an atom drawn as a cloud with a dot, and the dot opened to show protons and neutrons.
items.why: Each circle is many times smaller than the one before. The atom should be a cloud, and the nucleus a tiny ball of protons and neutrons.
items.art: Six empty circles in a row, getting smaller.

experiments.title: Cut It in Half, Again and Again
experiments.context: In this experiment you cut a strip of paper in half, then cut one half in half, again and again. You count the cuts and measure each piece. It shows how small things can get, and how far away atoms still are.
experiments.question: How many times can you cut a strip of paper in half?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many times do you think you can cut the strip in half before the piece is too small to cut? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason down.
experiments.fair_test: Always cut the piece exactly in half, across its width, and measure it with a ruler. Always keep one half and cut that one next. Count every cut. If you try again, use the same kind of paper and the same scissors.
results_table: Length of the piece (cm or mm)
Could you still hold it easily? Yes or no

materials.item: a strip of paper 24 cm long and 2 cm wide, cut from the long side of an A4 sheet or a notebook page
scissors for the child, and sharp scissors for the grown-up
a ruler
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Hold the paper by its long end, away from the blades. A grown-up does the cuts once the piece is shorter than 1 cm.

schedule.what: Guess, cut the strip in half again and again, measure each piece, and look at the last piece with a magnifier.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a line on a graph for how long the piece was after each cut.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: how long the piece was after each cut
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what your results may look like. Each cut halves the piece. After 8 cuts it is about 1 millimetre long.

flow.do: 1. Cut a strip of paper 24 cm long and 2 cm wide. 2. Put the strip, scissors, ruler and results table on a table. 3. Ask your child to guess how many cuts they will manage.
flow.say: We'll cut this strip in half, then cut one half in half, again and again. How many cuts do you think we can do before it's too small?
flow.kid: Here is a strip of paper, 24 cm long. You will cut it in half again and again. How many cuts can you do? Write your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cut It in Half. You cut a strip of paper in half again and again, to see how small you can go.

flow.do: 1. Fold the strip in half to find the middle. 2. Cut across the strip at the fold. 3. Measure one half and write the length in the table. 4. Keep one half and cut it in half the same way. 5. Do this 4 times. The piece is now 1 and a half centimetres long.
flow.say: Each time, we cut across the strip, so the piece stays 2 centimetres wide. That gives you an edge to hold. Measure it and write it down.
flow.kid: Fold the strip to find the middle. Cut across it. Measure one half. Keep it and cut it in half again.
flow.parent: The lengths should be 12 cm, 6 cm, 3 cm and then 1 and a half cm. Cutting across the strip keeps one long edge of 2 cm, so small fingers stay away from the blades.

check.q: The strip was 24 cm long. How long is one piece after the first cut?
check.why: Cutting in half makes two equal pieces. 24 divided by 2 is 12. So each piece is 12 cm long. Picking 48 cm usually means mixing up halving with doubling.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up now holds the piece by its 2 cm edge and cuts it in half with sharp scissors. 2. Measure with the millimetre marks on the ruler. 3. Keep going until the piece is too thin to cut, usually after 7 to 9 cuts.
flow.say: Now the pieces are tiny, so I'll do the cutting. Count with me. Cut five. Cut six. Is it getting hard?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to do the tiny cuts. Count each cut out loud. When does it get too small?
flow.parent: After 8 cuts, the piece is a thin sliver about 1 millimetre wide. If the sliver slips, press it under a fingertip on a cutting board and cut beside your finger. Stop when it cannot be cut cleanly. Most people stop at 7, 8 or 9.

flow.do: 1. Look at the cut edge of the last sliver with a magnifying glass, or a zoomed-in phone camera. 2. Look for tiny threads sticking out.
flow.say: Look at the edge. Can you see tiny threads? Paper is made of plant fibres. Each fibre is made of molecules, and each molecule is made of atoms.
flow.kid: Look at the edge with a magnifier. Can you see tiny threads? Paper is made of them. The threads are made of atoms.

ask.q: We stopped after about 8 cuts. How many more cuts would it take to make the piece one atom wide?

flow.parent: To make the piece just one atom wide, you would need about 31 cuts in all. So everyone is still about 23 cuts away when the scissors stop. Show the halving chart on the 'How small is an atom?' card.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What do you think? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: paper is made of particles much too small to cut with scissors. What I saw: I cut it 8 times, and the last piece was about 1 millimetre. Under the magnifier I saw tiny threads. Why: the threads are made of molecules, and molecules are made of atoms. A piece one atom wide is still about 23 cuts away.

experiments.title: The Hidden Centre: roll marbles like Rutherford
experiments.context: Scientists found the tiny centre of the atom without seeing it, by firing alpha particles at gold and watching which came back. In this experiment you do the same with marbles. You roll them under a card and work out what is hidden there, without looking.
experiments.question: Can you find out the size of a hidden thing just by rolling marbles at it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If the hidden thing is very small, how many of 20 marbles will come back? If it is big, how many? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Roll every marble the same way: from the same edge, at the same gentle speed, at a different spot along the edge each time. Roll 20 marbles each time. Only the hidden thing changes.

materials.item: a big flat piece of cardboard, about 50 cm by 50 cm, such as a flattened carton
4 steel tumblers or 4 equal stacks of books, to hold the card up at the corners
about 10 marbles, or small rubber balls
things to hide: a big steel bowl turned upside down, and one AA battery standing on its end in a small ball of chapati dough, so it cannot fall over
a smooth floor, such as tiles or stone

experiments.safety: Pick up every marble afterwards, so nobody slips on them. Marbles are a choking risk for children under 3.

schedule.what: Roll marbles at two hidden things. Count what comes back. Guess what each hidden thing is, then look.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for each hidden thing. Draw the card from above, with arrows showing where the marbles went.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: 20 marbles rolled under the card each time

flow.do: 1. Put the four tumblers on a smooth floor, about 45 cm apart, in a square. 2. While your child looks away, put the upside-down bowl in the middle. 3. Lay the cardboard on top of the tumblers, so it hides the bowl.
flow.say: Something is hidden under this card. You may not look or touch it. You can only roll marbles under the card and watch what comes out.
flow.kid: Something is hidden under the card. Don't peek! You can only roll marbles under it. Watch where they come out.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Hidden Centre. You hide something under a card held up by four tumblers, so that marbles can roll underneath.

flow.do: 1. Your child kneels at one side and rolls a marble gently under the card. 2. Watch where it comes out: straight across, off to one side, or back towards them. 3. Make a tally mark in the right column. 4. Roll 20 marbles, from different spots along the edge.
flow.say: Roll gently, a different spot each time. Did it go straight through? Turn aside? Or come back to you?
flow.kid: Roll a marble under the card. Where did it come out? Make a tally mark. Roll 20 marbles, a new spot each time.
flow.parent: A big bowl usually turns several marbles aside, and sends a few straight back. If marbles stop on a rug, move to a smooth floor. If they roll over the hidden thing, use something taller.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess how big the hidden thing is and where it sits. 2. Then lift the card and look.
flow.say: From what the marbles did, how big do you think the hidden thing is? Where is it? Let's look.
flow.kid: Guess: is the hidden thing big or small? Where is it? Now lift the card and see!

flow.do: 1. While your child looks away, swap the bowl for one AA battery. 2. Press its bottom end into a small ball of chapati dough, so it stands up firmly. 3. Put the card back. 4. Roll 20 marbles again and tally.
flow.say: Now something much smaller is hidden. Roll 20 marbles again. What happens this time?
flow.kid: Now something smaller is hidden. Roll 20 marbles again. How many come back now?

check.q: With a tiny battery hidden, what happened to most marbles?
check.why: Most of the space under the card was empty, so most marbles missed the battery. Only one or two hit it and turned or bounced back. This is what happened in 1909, when alpha particles were fired at gold. Most went straight through, and very few came back. So each atom must be mostly empty, with a tiny, heavy centre. Picking 'they all came back' usually means picturing the hidden thing as a wall, the way scientists pictured atoms before 1909.

chart.title: Made-up example: what happened to 20 marbles when one battery was hidden

flow.parent: With the battery, only 1 or 2 marbles in 20 usually hit it. Most of those turn aside, and only a head-on hit comes back. If none hit it, roll 20 more.

flow.do: Tell your child how the real experiment worked, using the 'An atom is almost all empty space' card.
flow.say: In 1909, scientists fired alpha particles at very thin gold. Almost all went straight through. About 1 in 8,000 came back. What does that tell us about atoms?
flow.kid: Scientists did this with gold in 1909. Almost everything went straight through. Only 1 in 8,000 bounced back. What does that tell you?
flow.think: Your battery was hit by about 1 marble in 20. The real nucleus was hit by about 1 in 8,000. Which is emptier, your card or a gold atom?

experiments.title: Colour Spreads by Itself
experiments.context: In this experiment you put one drop of food colour into hot water and into cold water, without stirring. You watch the colour spread by itself. It shows that still water is never really still, and that warm water moves more.
experiments.question: Does colour spread through still water by itself? Does it spread faster in hot water or in cold water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the colour spread if nobody stirs it? In which glass will it spread faster: the hot one or the cold one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two glasses of the same size, with the same amount of water. Wait one minute so both are still. Add one drop to each at the same moment, from the same height. Do not stir or bump the table. Only the water's warmth changes.

materials.item: two clear glasses of the same size (not thin plastic cups, which go soft in hot water)
cold water from a clay pot or the fridge
hot water from a kettle, hot but not boiling
food colour, or a drop of fountain-pen ink, or a few grains of instant coffee
a white sheet of paper to put behind and under the glasses
a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Let the kettle water cool for 2 minutes first, so the glass does not crack. Don't touch the hot glass.

schedule.what: Drop colour into hot and cold water and watch for 5 minutes, without stirring.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both glasses at 1, 3 and 5 minutes.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: one drop of food colour, no stirring
rows: Colour swirling through half the glass
Nearly all the glass is coloured
A thin stream sinking to the bottom
A coloured layer at the bottom
Still mostly clear at the top

flow.do: 1. Put the two glasses side by side on the white paper, on a table nobody will bump. 2. Fill one with cold water. 3. A grown-up fills the other with hot water to the same level. 4. Wait one minute until both are still.
flow.say: This glass is cold and this one is hot. We'll wait one minute so the water stops moving.
flow.kid: Put two clear glasses on white paper. A grown-up fills one with hot water. You fill the other with cold. Wait one minute.
flow.context: This is the first step of Colour Spreads by Itself. You set up a glass of hot water and a glass of cold water side by side.

flow.do: 1. Hold the food colour just above the water. 2. Drop one drop into each glass at the same moment. 3. Do not stir. 4. Watch and draw at 1, 3 and 5 minutes.
flow.say: One drop in each, at the same time. Now hands off the table. What do you see?
flow.kid: Drop one drop of colour in each glass at the same time. Don't stir! Watch closely and draw what you see.

ask.q: Nobody is stirring. So what is moving the colour?

flow.parent: In the hot glass, the colour usually swirls through most of the water within 2 or 3 minutes. In the cold glass, it sinks in a thin stream and is still patchy after 5 minutes. Most of the hot glass's swirling is warm water rising and cooler water sinking. This is called convection. Molecules bumping alone would take hours to colour the glass, but they do blur the colour's edges.

flow.do: Talk about what made the colour spread, using the 'How we know atoms are real' card.
flow.say: Nobody stirred, but the water was moving. In the hot glass, warm water rises and cooler water sinks, so the water stirs itself. This is called convection. Water is also made of molecules that never stop moving. They bump the colour and blur its edges. In hot water, they move faster.
flow.kid: Nobody stirred, but the water moved. Hot water stirs itself. Warm water rises and cool water sinks. Water molecules never stop moving, too. Hot ones move faster!

check.q: Why did the colour spread faster in the hot water?
options: Hot water moves more: it swirls as warm water rises, and its molecules move faster
The drop fell harder into the hot glass
check.why: Hot water stirs itself: warm water rises and cooler water sinks, which is called convection. Its molecules also move faster, so they bump the colour around faster. Picking 'hot water is thinner' is a sensible guess, because hot water does flow a little more easily. Picking 'the drop fell harder' misses that both drops fell from the same height.

activities.title: Pencil Dots: draw an electron cloud
activities.context: In this activity you close your eyes and try to hit a target with a pencil, 50 times. The dots make a cloud. It is a picture of how scientists draw where an electron is likely to be found.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with a bindi, a sticker or a small drawn dot in the middle
a sharp pencil
a bangle and a bigger bangle or a steel plate, to draw rings

activities.safety: Keep the pencil point down, away from eyes.

schedule.what: Make 50 dots with eyes closed, draw rings and count the dots in each ring.

activities.record: Count the dots in each ring and write the numbers. Draw a bar for each ring.

flow.do: 1. Put the paper flat on a table, with the target in the middle. 2. Show your child how to lift the pencil to their ear, close their eyes, and dot.
flow.say: Look at the target. Lift the pencil up to your ear. Close your eyes. Now bring it down and make a dot where you think the target is.
flow.kid: Look at the target dot. Lift your pencil up to your ear. Close your eyes. Bring the pencil down to make a dot!
flow.context: This is the first step of Pencil Dots. You make pencil dots with your eyes closed, to build a picture like an electron cloud.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes 50 dots, eyes closed every time. 2. Open your eyes between dots only to look at the target again. 3. Count out loud together.
flow.say: Keep going until we have 50 dots. Look at the target, close your eyes, dot. Count with me.
flow.kid: Make 50 dots. Look, close your eyes, dot. Count out loud as you go.
flow.parent: Some dots will land near the target and a few far away. That is good. If a child peeks, it still works, as long as they keep the pencil moving from the ear each time.

flow.do: 1. Put the small bangle around the target and draw a ring. 2. Use a bigger bangle or a plate to draw a second ring, and a bigger plate for a third. 3. Count the dots in each ring.
flow.say: Let's draw rings around the target and count. Which ring has the most dots? Where are the dots packed most tightly?
flow.kid: Draw rings with a bangle and a plate. Count the dots in each ring. Where are they packed most tightly?

chart.title: Made-up example: where 50 pencil dots landed
chart.note: The inner ring is also the smallest ring. So the dots are packed most tightly near the target.

flow.do: Explain the link to electrons, using the 'Electrons are found in clouds, not on tracks' card.
flow.say: Each dot is like one measurement of an electron. One measurement finds it at one spot. Many measurements make a cloud, thick in the middle. Scientists draw atoms just like this.
flow.kid: Each dot is like finding an electron once. Many dots make a cloud. That is how scientists draw electrons!

check.q: Could you have said exactly where your next dot would land?
options: No, only that it would probably be near the target
No, it could be anywhere with the same chance
check.why: You could say the dot would probably be near the target, but not exactly where. That is how scientists treat an electron. They know the chances of each place, never the next spot for sure. Picking 'anywhere with the same chance' misses that the dots were thickest near the target.

flow.think: Your dots were spread out because your hand wobbled. An electron's cloud is not caused by wobbling. In quantum physics, the chance is part of nature itself. Does that seem strange to you?

activities.title: A Mustard-Seed Atom (if you have a park or a long corridor)
activities.context: In this activity you make a giant model of an atom outdoors. A mustard seed is the nucleus. You walk out to find where the atom's edge would be. It shows how empty an atom is.

materials.item: a few mustard seeds (rai) on a coin or a small plate
a park, a playground, a long corridor or a quiet lane
a dupatta, a stick or a chappal to mark the edge

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up, and keep away from traffic.

schedule.what: Put a mustard seed in the middle of a park and walk out to the edge of the 'atom'.

activities.record: Draw the park, the seed in the middle and the atom's edge. Write how many steps you walked.

flow.do: 1. Put a mustard seed on a coin in the middle of an open space. 2. Show your child how tiny it is.
flow.say: This mustard seed is the nucleus, the centre of our atom. Remember, it holds nearly all the atom's weight.
flow.kid: This mustard seed is the nucleus. It is the centre of your atom. It holds nearly all the atom's weight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Mustard-Seed Atom. You make a model of an atom as big as a park, with a mustard seed at its centre.

flow.do: 1. Walk away from the seed together in a straight line, counting steps. 2. Stop at about 30 metres, roughly 50 to 60 of a child's steps, or one and a half cricket pitches. 3. Put down the dupatta or stick there. That is the edge of the atom.
flow.say: Let's walk out to the edge of our atom. Count your steps. We need to go about as far as one and a half cricket pitches.
flow.kid: Walk away from the seed in a straight line. Count your steps. Keep going! Stop at about 50 or 60 steps.
flow.parent: Different atoms have different sizes, so these numbers are rough. For a mustard seed nucleus, the atom would reach roughly 25 to 30 metres in every direction. If you only have a corridor, walk to the end and say the atom goes even further.

ask.q: Turn around. Can you still see the seed?
good: I can only see the coin.

flow.do: Stand at the edge and look back. Talk about what is in between.
flow.say: The electron cloud spreads through all this space, from the seed out to here. But electrons are tiny, so there is almost nothing in it. That is empty space.
flow.kid: The electrons are spread through all this space. They are tiny. So it is almost all empty space!

check.q: In your park-sized atom, how much is empty space?
check.why: The seed is tiny, and the electrons are tiny too, spread thinly through the space. So almost all of it is empty. A real atom is the same, only far smaller. Picking 'packed full' is the old idea that atoms are solid balls. Experiments in 1909 showed they are not.

flow.do: Walk back to the seed and press your hand on the ground.
flow.say: The ground feels solid. But every atom in it is like our park: a tiny seed and lots of empty space. What you feel is electrons pushing back.
flow.kid: Press your hand on the ground. It feels solid. But it is almost all empty space! You feel electrons pushing back.
flow.think: If everything is almost all empty space, what does 'solid' really mean?

setup.caption: 1. Put a mustard seed in the middle of an open space.

setup.art: A child and parent walking away in a straight line, counting steps, the coin now a tiny glint behind them.
setup.caption: 2. Walk about 30 metres, counting your steps.

setup.caption: 3. Mark the edge of the atom. Look back. Can you see the seed?

activities.title: Dots Make Pictures
activities.context: In this activity you look very closely at a newspaper photo and a phone screen, and find that pictures are made of tiny dots. Then you make your own dot picture. It shows how many tiny dots can make one whole picture.

materials.item: a newspaper with a colour photo
a magnifying glass, or a drop of water on a clear plastic sheet
a phone with its screen on, and a few drops of water
cotton buds and paint, or felt pens, and paper
a few grains of salt and sugar on a dark plate

activities.safety: Use only one or two small drops of water on the phone screen, and wipe it dry straight after. A grown-up holds the phone.

schedule.what: Look closely at a newspaper photo, a phone screen and salt grains. Then make a dot picture.

activities.record: Draw what the photo looked like up close. Make one picture using only dots.

flow.do: 1. Look at a colour newspaper photo through the magnifier. 2. No magnifier? Put a drop of water on a clear plastic sheet and hold it just above the photo. The drop works like a small lens.
flow.say: From far away it looks like a photo. Look closer. What is it really made of?
flow.kid: Look at a newspaper photo through a magnifier. What do you see up close? Dots!
flow.context: This is the first step of Dots Make Pictures. You look closely at pictures to find the tiny dots they are made of.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts one small drop of water on a white part of a phone screen. 2. Look through the drop from the side and from above. 3. Wipe the screen dry.
flow.say: Look through the water drop. What colours can you see? A white screen is really made of tiny red, green and blue dots.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to drop water on a phone screen. Look through it. What colours do you see?
flow.parent: The drop acts as a lens. On most phone screens you will see tiny red, green and blue lights. Wipe the screen dry straight after.

flow.do: Look at grains of salt and sugar on a dark plate through the magnifier.
flow.say: Salt grains are little cubes. That shape comes from the way their atoms are stacked, in neat rows, like a box of laddoos.
flow.kid: Look at salt through the magnifier. Can you see little cubes? Their atoms are stacked in neat rows.

check.q: Why are salt grains shaped like little cubes?
options: Their atoms are stacked in neat, square rows
The factory cuts them into cubes
They were squashed in the packet
check.why: Salt is made of two kinds of atom, sodium and chlorine. They stack in a neat, square pattern, so the grains grow as cubes. Picking 'the factory cuts them' is a fair guess, because packets are made in factories. But salt crystals from the sea grow as cubes all by themselves.

flow.parent: The cubes are easiest to see in coarse salt, such as khada namak or sea salt. In fine packet salt, many grains are tiny or broken.

flow.do: Your child makes a picture using only dots. A mango, a face or a tree all work. Then stand back two metres and look.
flow.say: Make a picture using only dots, no lines. Then let's stand back. Up close it's dots. From far away it's a picture.
flow.kid: Make a picture with only dots. No lines! Then stand far back. What do you see?
flow.think: Everything is made of atoms too small to see, a little like your dots. Is the picture in the dots, or in how they are arranged?

setup.art: A child holding a magnifying glass over a colour newspaper photo, a zoomed circle showing tiny coloured dots.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a newspaper photo up close. It is made of dots.

setup.art: A drop of water on a white phone screen, with tiny red, green and blue lights showing through it.
setup.caption: 2. A drop of water on a phone screen shows its tiny coloured lights.

setup.art: A child dabbing paint dots with a cotton bud to make a picture of a mango.
setup.caption: 3. Make your own picture using only dots.

activities.title: Pushing Without Touching
activities.context: In this activity you feel two magnets push each other apart before they touch. It is a hand-sized model of why things feel solid, even though atoms are almost all empty space.

materials.item: two bar magnets or two round ring magnets
or: two balloons, two threads and dry hair or a woollen sweater

activities.safety: Keep magnets away from phones and bank cards. Pick up every bit of a popped balloon, as it is a choking risk for small children.

schedule.what: Feel magnets push apart without touching. Try rubbed balloons too.

activities.record: Draw the two magnets with arrows showing the push. Write one sentence about how it felt.

flow.do: 1. Hold one magnet in each hand. 2. Slowly bring the same ends together, north to north. 3. Feel the push before they touch. 4. Turn one around and feel them pull.
flow.say: Bring them close slowly. Can you feel them pushing? They haven't even touched.
flow.kid: Hold a magnet in each hand. Bring them close slowly. Feel the push? Now turn one around and try again.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pushing Without Touching. You feel two magnets push each other apart before they touch.

flow.do: 1. If you have no magnets, or want more: blow up two balloons and tie a thread to each. 2. Rub both on dry hair. 3. Hold them up by their threads, side by side.
flow.say: Both balloons now have extra electrons. Electrons repel each other: they push each other away. Watch the balloons lean apart.
flow.kid: Rub two balloons on dry hair. Hang them side by side. Do they lean apart?
flow.parent: Balloons work best on a dry day. In humid or monsoon weather they may not push much, so use magnets.

flow.do: Press your hand on the table. Explain the link to atoms, using the 'Why things feel solid' card.
flow.say: When your hand presses the table, the electrons in your hand push the table's electrons, like those magnets. That push is what 'solid' feels like.
flow.kid: Press your hand on the table. Its electrons push your hand's electrons. That push is what 'solid' feels like!

check.q: Atoms are almost all empty space. Why doesn't your hand sink into the table?
options: Electrons in your hand and the table push each other away
The table is packed solid with no gaps
check.why: Electrons all have a minus charge, and two minus charges repel. So your hand's electrons and the table's electrons push apart, very strongly. A quantum rule also stops electrons squeezing together. Picking 'packed solid' is the old idea of atoms as hard balls. Picking 'gravity' mixes things up, because gravity pulls your hand down, not up.

setup.art: Two hands bringing two bar magnets together end to end, small arrows showing them pushing apart in the gap.
setup.caption: 1. Bring the same ends of two magnets together. Feel the push.

setup.art: Two rubbed balloons hanging on threads, leaning away from each other.
setup.caption: 2. Or rub two balloons on dry hair and hang them side by side.

setup.art: A child's hand pressed on a table, a zoomed circle showing electron clouds pushing each other.
setup.caption: 3. Press the table. Electrons push back, like the magnets.

activities.title: The Smell Race
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up opens something with a strong smell at one end of a room, and everyone waits to smell it. It shows that molecules travel through the air to your nose, even though you cannot see them.

materials.item: something with a strong smell: a cut orange peel, a crushed clove of garlic, or a few drops of rose water
a room with the fan off and the windows closed
a phone timer

activities.safety: Do not use perfume sprays, incense or anything burning.

schedule.what: Time how long a smell takes to cross a still room.

activities.record: Write down where each person stood and how many seconds it took for them to smell it.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan and close the windows. 2. Everyone stands at different distances from one corner: 1 metre, 2 metres and as far as you can. 3. Everyone closes their eyes.
flow.say: Stand still and close your eyes. When you smell something, put your hand up. Don't peek!
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Stand still. Put your hand up when you smell something.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Smell Race. You time how long a smell takes to travel across a still room.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up in the corner squeezes the orange peel, or opens the rose water, and starts the timer. 2. Note the time each hand goes up.
flow.say: I'm starting the timer now. Hands up when you smell it.
flow.kid: Wait with your eyes closed. Can you smell it yet? Hand up when you do!
flow.parent: Times vary a lot, from a few seconds to a couple of minutes. The nearest person usually smells it first. Most of the travelling is done by small air currents, which carry the molecules along.

flow.do: Talk about what reached your nose.
flow.say: Nothing you could see crossed the room. But molecules from the orange peel did. Your nose caught some of them.
flow.kid: Nothing you could see crossed the room. But molecules from the orange did! Your nose caught them.

options: Molecules from the orange, too small to see
Nothing, a smell is not a thing
check.why: A smell is tiny molecules that float off the orange into the air. When some reach your nose, you smell them. Picking 'nothing' is a common idea, because a smell is invisible. But you can only smell something when its molecules arrive. Moving air carried most of them to you.

flow.think: Right now, molecules from many things around you are floating in the air. What else might you be breathing in?

setup.caption: 1. Switch off the fan. Stand at different distances. Close your eyes.

setup.art: A grown-up in the corner squeezing an orange peel, a faint mist of dots drifting from it, a phone timer on.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up squeezes an orange peel and starts the timer.

setup.art: The nearest child raising a hand, the dots of smell reaching her nose.
setup.caption: 3. Hand up when you smell it. Who smelled it first?

activities.title: Salt Turns the Flame Yellow: atoms on a staircase
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up sprinkles a pinch of salt on a gas flame, and it flashes bright yellow. Then you act out why on a staircase. It shows a strange rule of the very small: electrons can only have certain amounts of energy, like standing on steps.

materials.item: a gas stove, used only by a grown-up
a pinch of dry table salt on a spoon
a staircase or a few steps

activities.safety: Only a grown-up lights the stove and sprinkles the salt. The child watches from at least one metre away. Use dry salt only.

schedule.what: Watch salt turn a gas flame yellow, then play the staircase game.

activities.record: Draw the flame before and after the salt. Draw a staircase with an electron jumping down one step.

flow.do: 1. The child stands at least one metre from the stove. 2. A grown-up lights one burner on low. 3. The grown-up holds a spoon of dry salt high above the flame. 4. They tip it slowly, so a few grains fall in.
flow.say: Watch the blue flame. Now I'm sprinkling a few grains of salt. What colour do you see?
flow.kid: Stand back and watch the blue flame. A grown-up sprinkles salt. What colour flashes?
flow.parent: The flame flashes bright yellow-orange. That colour comes from sodium, one of the two kinds of atom in salt. Homes with induction cooktops have no flame. Instead, look at an old orange street light, which uses the same sodium yellow, or watch a flame test video.
flow.context: This is the first step of Salt Turns the Flame Yellow. A grown-up sprinkles a little salt on a gas flame, and you watch the colour.

flow.do: 1. Go to a staircase. 2. The child stands on the bottom step. That is the electron's usual place. 3. When you say 'Heat!', they jump up one step. 4. When you say 'Let go!', they jump down and call out 'Yellow!'. 5. Ask them to try standing halfway between two steps.
flow.say: You're an electron in a sodium atom. The flame's heat lifts you up one step. When you jump down, you give out a flash of yellow light. Can you stand between two steps?
flow.kid: You are an electron! 'Heat!' Jump up one step. 'Let go!' Jump down and shout 'Yellow!' Can you stand between steps?
flow.parent: Electrons in an atom can only have certain amounts of energy, like standing on steps, never in between. Each drop down a step gives out light of one exact colour. Sodium's brightest light is yellow. A ball rolling down a ramp can stop anywhere. This is one way the very small does not behave like the things we see.

flow.do: Talk about where else this happens.
flow.say: Every kind of atom has its own staircase, so it gives out its own colours. Fireworks use this. Copper gives blue-green, and strontium gives red.
flow.kid: Every kind of atom has its own colours. Fireworks use this! Copper makes blue-green. Strontium makes red.

check.q: Why does salt make the flame yellow?
options: Electrons in its sodium atoms jump down one step and give out yellow light
check.why: The heat lifts electrons in the sodium atoms up an energy step. When they drop back down, each gives out a tiny flash of light of one exact colour, a yellow. Picking 'salt burns like wood' is a sensible guess about flames. But the salt is not burning. Its atoms are glowing.

flow.think: Astronomers see these same colours in starlight, and that is how they know what stars are made of. Meghnad Saha, an Indian scientist, worked out in 1920 how to read star temperatures from them.

setup.caption: 2. You are an electron. 'Heat!' Jump up one step.

projects.title: Make an Honest Carbon Atom
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a model of a carbon atom, the kind of atom in a pencil tip and in every living thing. Instead of planets on tracks, you give it an honest electron cloud.

materials.item: 6 dark brown tamarind seeds and 6 white chana, or two colours of clay balls
a little glue or a ball of chapati dough to stick them together
a paper plate or a round piece of card
a handful of cotton wool
a black or blue sketch pen and labels

projects.safety: Small beans and seeds are a choking risk for children under 3. Wash hands after using chapati dough.

schedule.what: Build the nucleus from 6 tamarind seeds and 6 chana. Leave the glue to dry overnight.
Make the electron cloud from cotton and pen dots. Label the model and explain it to someone.

projects.record: Draw your model and label the nucleus, protons, neutrons and electron cloud. Write one sentence about what your model gets wrong.

flow.do: Look at the 'What an atom is made of' card together. Count out 6 tamarind seeds for protons and 6 chana for neutrons.
flow.say: A carbon atom has 6 protons and 6 neutrons in its nucleus. The tamarind seeds are the protons. The chana are the neutrons.
flow.kid: Count 6 dark tamarind seeds. These are protons. Count 6 white chana. These are neutrons.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make an Honest Carbon Atom. You count out beans to build the centre of a carbon atom.

flow.do: 1. Press the tamarind seeds and chana together into a small ball, using glue or a little chapati dough. 2. Mix the colours. 3. Put it in the middle of the paper plate.
flow.say: Press them together into one little ball. This is the nucleus, the heavy centre of the atom.
flow.kid: Squeeze the beans into one little ball. Mix the colours. Put it in the middle of the plate.
flow.parent: Real protons and neutrons are jumbled together like this, not in neat rows.

flow.do: Leave the nucleus to dry overnight.
flow.say: We'll let it dry. Tomorrow we'll give it its electrons.
flow.kid: Let it dry until tomorrow. Next, you will make the electrons.
flow.wait: Leave the glue to dry for 1 day.

flow.do: 1. Pull the cotton wool apart into a thin, fluffy ring around the nucleus. 2. Make it thickest close to the nucleus and thinnest at the edge. 3. Dot the plate with pen dots, many near the middle and few at the edge.
flow.say: Electrons don't go round on tracks. So instead of drawing rings, we'll make a cloud. Thick where the electrons are often found. Thin where they're rarely found.
flow.kid: Fluff the cotton into a cloud around the nucleus. Thick near the middle. Thin at the edge. Add pen dots too.

check.q: Why is our model a cloud, not rings like planets?
options: Electrons have no tracks. We can only say where they are likely to be.
check.why: Quantum physics shows that electrons do not move on tracks. It gives the chances of finding them in each place. A cloud shows that best: thick where they are likely, thin where they are not. Picking 'easier to make' misses the science. Rings would actually be quicker, but they would be wrong.

flow.do: 1. Label the parts. 2. Ask your child to say what the model gets wrong. 3. Your child explains the model to someone else in the family.
flow.say: Every model is wrong somewhere. If our nucleus were this size, how big would the real cloud be?
flow.kid: Label your model. Then think: what does it get wrong? Explain your atom to someone at home.
flow.parent: Good answers: the nucleus is far too big for the cloud. If this bean nucleus were real, its electron cloud would be about a kilometre across. Real atoms have no colours. The electrons are not cotton.
flow.think: Scientists use models they know are not quite right. Why might a wrong model still be useful?

setup.caption: 2. Press them into one small ball: the nucleus.

challenges.title: Prove the Invisible
challenges.problem: Your friend says, 'Air is nothing. You can't see it, so it isn't there.' Prove to them that air is real matter, made of molecules too small to see, using only things from home.
constraints: You may not just say 'my teacher told me'.
You must use at least two different tests.
Each test must be safe to do indoors.
materials: a clear glass, a bucket or bowl of water and a dry tissue
general: Blow up a balloon. The air pushes the balloon out, so air takes up space.
Push a tissue into the bottom of a glass. Turn the glass upside down and push it straight down into water. The tissue stays dry, because air fills the glass.
Squeeze an empty plastic bottle with the cap on. The air inside pushes back.
creative: Do the smell race. Molecules from an orange peel travel through the air to your nose.
Wave a big piece of cardboard fast. You can feel the air push against it. Something that pushes must be there.
Put a blown-up balloon in the fridge for an hour. It shrinks a little, because the cold air molecules move more slowly and push less on the rubber.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own test that proves air is there. Try it, and see if your friend is convinced.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to say what the friend believes, and why it seems true.
flow.say: Your friend says air is nothing, because you can't see it. Why might someone think that? How could we prove them wrong?
flow.kid: Your friend says air is nothing. Why might they think so? How could you prove them wrong?
flow.context: This is the first step of Prove the Invisible. It is a challenge to prove that air is real matter, made of molecules too small to see.

flow.do: 1. Push a dry tissue into the bottom of a glass. 2. Turn it upside down and push it straight down into a bowl of water. 3. Lift it straight out and feel the tissue. 4. Try one more test of your choice.
flow.say: If air is nothing, the water should rush in and wet the tissue. Let's see what happens.
flow.kid: Push a tissue into a glass. Turn it upside down and push it into water. Lift it out. Is the tissue dry?

options: Air filled the glass, so the water couldn't get in
check.why: Air is made of molecules, and they take up space. They filled the glass, so there was no room for the water. Picking 'the tissue is waterproof' is easy to test: dip the tissue in water and it gets wet at once.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas. Then invent a new test.
flow.say: Here are the usual tests and some creative ones. Can you invent a test nobody has thought of?
flow.kid: Look at the usual tests and some creative ones. Now invent your own!
flow.think: Scientists proved atoms are real without ever seeing one. What else might be real but invisible?

setup.caption: 1. Push a dry tissue into the bottom of a glass.

setup.caption: 2. Push it upside down into water.

challenges.title: Write It Smaller
challenges.problem: In 1989, scientists wrote the letters IBM using just 35 single atoms. How small can YOU write your initials, so that someone can still read them with a magnifying glass?
constraints: Someone else must be able to read your letters with a magnifier.
Measure your letters with a ruler.
materials: a very sharp pencil and a fine pen
mustard seeds and grains of salt
general: Sharpen the pencil to a fine point and write slowly.
Rest your writing hand on the table so it does not wobble.
Use smooth, hard paper, so the lines stay thin.
creative: Spell your first letter with mustard seeds, then with grains of salt. Which letter is smaller?
Write on a grain of rice. In India, some artists write whole names on single rice grains.
Use a needle dipped in ink, held by a grown-up, for the thinnest lines.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to write even smaller. Measure your letters. How many atoms wide would they be?

flow.do: Tell your child about the IBM letters, using the 'How we know atoms are real' card.
flow.say: Scientists moved single atoms with a super-sharp needle, and spelled three letters. How small do you think you can write?
flow.kid: Scientists spelled IBM with 35 single atoms! How small can you write your initials?
flow.context: This is the first step of Write It Smaller. It is a challenge to write your initials as small as you can, inspired by scientists who wrote with single atoms.

flow.do: 1. Write your initials normal size. 2. Then smaller, and smaller again. 3. Measure the smallest readable letters with a ruler. 4. Try the creative ideas.
flow.say: Write it smaller each time. Can I still read it with the magnifier? Let's measure your smallest letter.
flow.kid: Write your initials smaller, then smaller still! Can someone read them with a magnifier? Measure the smallest.
flow.parent: Most children can write readable letters about 2 millimetres tall, and some get to 1 millimetre. If you use a needle, the grown-up holds it.

flow.do: Compare your smallest letter with atoms.
flow.say: Your letter is about 1 or 2 millimetres tall. About 5 million atoms fit across 1 millimetre. How many atoms tall is your letter?
flow.kid: Your letter is about 1 millimetre tall. That is about 5 million atoms! How many is that for your letter?

check.q: A letter is 2 millimetres tall. About 5 million atoms fit across 1 millimetre. About how many atoms tall is the letter?
check.why: Each millimetre is about 5 million atoms. Two millimetres is 5 million plus 5 million, which is about 10 million. Picking 2 or 7 usually means mixing up millimetres and atoms. Atoms are far, far smaller.

flow.think: The scientists' letters were only a few atoms tall. What could you build if you could move single atoms?

videos.title: The Double Slit Experiment, with Jim Al-Khalili
videos.why: For the parent and curious older children: a physicist explains how electrons and light spread like waves but land as dots. Watch with the 'observer' card in mind. In physics, 'looking' means measuring with a detector, not only with a person's eyes.
videos.check: Found by YouTube search in this session: title 'Why reality changes when you look at it | The Double Slit Experiment | with Jim Al-Khalili' by The Royal Institution, 9 minutes 8 seconds. quiz.why: All matter, including air and you, is made of atoms. Picking 'only what we can see' is natural, because atoms are invisible. Light is not made of atoms, so it cannot be what everything is made of.

quiz.p: Can you see one atom with a magnifying glass?
opts: No, atoms are far too small
quiz.why: An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. A magnifying glass only makes things a few times bigger. Picking 'only in sunlight' is a guess that more light helps. It doesn't, because light waves are thousands of times longer than an atom is wide.

quiz.p: In the paper-cutting experiment, the piece became too small to cut after about 8 cuts. Had you reached an atom?
opts: No, you were still about 23 cuts away
No, you could never reach one
quiz.why: To get a piece one atom wide from a 24 cm strip takes about 31 halvings. So 8 cuts still leaves about 23 to go. Picking 'yes' is very common, because the last piece looks so tiny. It still had millions of atoms across it.
quiz.context: This question is about the paper-cutting experiment. You cut a 24 cm strip of paper in half, then cut one half in half, again and again.

quiz.why: A virus is about a thousand times bigger across than an atom, and a grain of salt is far bigger again. Picking 'a virus' usually means thinking that germs are the smallest things there are.

quiz.p: What is in the nucleus of an atom?
quiz.why: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons. Electrons are found around it. Picking 'air' is a mix-up, because air is itself made of atoms.

quiz.p: What decides whether an atom is carbon, gold or oxygen?
quiz.why: Carbon has 6 protons, oxygen 8 and gold 79. Picking 'its colour' is a sensible guess, because gold looks golden. But single atoms have no colour of their own like that.

quiz.p: Scientists fired alpha particles at thin metal. Almost all went straight through. What did that show?
opts: Atoms are almost all empty space
The alpha particles were too small to matter
quiz.why: If almost everything passes through, there is almost nothing there to hit. The rare bounce showed a tiny, heavy centre. Picking 'metal is soft' misses why a few alpha particles came flying back.

quiz.p: In the marble test with a tiny battery hidden, most marbles went straight through and one came back. What is the battery like in a real atom?
quiz.why: The small, hard battery is like the tiny, heavy nucleus. Most marbles missed it, as most alpha particles missed the nucleus. Picking 'an electron' is a fair guess, but electrons are far too light to throw back an alpha particle.
quiz.context: This question is about the marble test. You hide something under a card held up on four tumblers, then roll marbles under it and watch where they come out.

quiz.p: How do electrons move in an atom?
opts: Round and round on tracks, like planets
We can only say where they are likely to be found, like a cloud
They sit still on the nucleus
quiz.why: Quantum physics gives the chances of finding an electron in each place, so scientists draw a cloud. Picking 'like planets' is the old 1913 picture that is still in many books and logos.

quiz.p: In the pencil-dot activity, 50 dots made a cloud, thickest near the target. What is that cloud like?
opts: An electron cloud: one dot is like one measurement
quiz.why: Each dot is one 'finding'. Many findings make a cloud of chances, just like the picture of an electron. Picking 'a real electron' takes the model too literally. The dots are a picture of chances.
quiz.context: This question is about the pencil-dot activity. You close your eyes and try to dot a target 50 times, then count the dots in rings around it.

quiz.p: In physics, what can be an 'observer'?
opts: Anything that measures, like a detector or a beam of light
Only a scientist with a notebook
quiz.why: Anything that a particle bumps into can measure it. No person is needed. Picking 'only a person' comes from the everyday meaning of the word. Experiments work the same with no person in the room.

quiz.p: Does quantum physics prove that our minds make the world real?
opts: Only for big things like tables
quiz.why: Physicists still argue about what measurement means. But none of the main ideas needs a person watching, and experiments work without anyone watching. Picking 'yes' is understandable, because some films and books say so. They mix up the physics word 'observer' with its everyday meaning.

quiz.p: How did scientists first become sure that atoms are real?
opts: From what atoms do, like jiggling tiny specks in water
Someone saw one with their eyes
quiz.why: Einstein in 1905 and Perrin in 1908 showed that tiny specks jiggle because invisible molecules bump them. Picking 'Kanada told them' misses that an idea needs evidence. Kanada's idea was brilliant, but proof came over 2,000 years later.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know?
opts: What an electron is doing between measurements
quiz.why: Atoms and nuclei are settled science. What happens between measurements is still argued over. Picking 'whether atoms exist' was a fair question in 1900, but it was settled by 1908.

applications: Phone chips, computers and LED lights were designed using quantum physics, the science of the very small.
Atomic clocks keep time using the exact energy steps of caesium atoms. The CSIR-National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi keeps Indian Standard Time with them.
India's NavIC navigation satellites carry atomic clocks to tell your phone where you are.
Scanning tunnelling microscopes picture and move single atoms, to design new materials.
Fireworks get their colours from different atoms: sodium for yellow, copper for blue-green, strontium for red.
Astronomers read the colours in starlight to find out which atoms stars are made of.
Solar panels turn light into electricity, because light knocks electrons loose.
Hospitals use MRI scanners, which read the tiny spins of hydrogen nuclei in your body to make pictures.
Lasers, used in barcode scanners and eye surgery, work because electrons drop down exact energy steps.
Nuclear power stations, like the ones at Tarapur and Kudankulam, get energy from splitting the nuclei of atoms.
Medicines are designed by working out the shapes of molecules, atom by atom.
Electron microscopes use beams of electrons, instead of light, to see things far smaller than a cell.

open_questions.q: What is an electron doing between measurements?
open_questions.why_open: The maths predicts every experiment perfectly. But scientists still argue about what is really happening when nothing measures it.
Electrons and quarks have no size that anyone has found. Nobody knows if there is anything smaller inside them.

open_questions.q: Are particles really little things, or ripples in invisible fields?
open_questions.why_open: Many physicists think fields are what the world is really made of. What the fields themselves are, nobody knows.
It is the idea that the smallest particles are tiny vibrating strings. No experiment has been able to test it yet.

open_questions.q: Why does the universe have more matter than antimatter?
open_questions.why_open: Every particle has an opposite twin. The Big Bang should have made equal amounts, which would destroy each other. Somehow a little matter was left over, and nobody knows why.

open_questions.q: What is most of the universe made of?
open_questions.why_open: All the atoms we know make up only about a sixth of the matter in the universe. The rest, called dark matter, has never been seen directly.

open_questions.q: Why do big things look so sure and solid, when tiny things follow rules of chance?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand a lot of this: bumps with the world around them hide the chance in big things. But exactly where the tiny world ends and the everyday world begins is still studied.

open_questions.q: When did Kanada live, and what exactly did he teach?
open_questions.why_open: Very old texts are hard to date, and his teachings come to us through later writers.

maths.problem: Your strip of paper is 24 cm long. You cut it in half, then cut one half in half, then cut one of those in half. How long is your piece now? What fraction of the strip is it?
maths.answer: 3 cm, which is one eighth of the strip.
maths.explain: After the first cut, the piece is half the strip: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm. After the second cut, it is half of a half, which is a quarter: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm. After the third cut, it is half of a quarter, which is an eighth: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm. Check: 8 pieces of 3 cm make 24 cm.
maths.context: This is about the paper-cutting experiment. You cut a 24 cm strip in half, then keep one half and cut it in half again, and so on.
maths.why_maths: Each cut takes a half of what is left. Fractions tell you how much of the whole strip you still have, so you can see how fast things shrink.

maths.problem: Look at the line graph of the paper-cutting results. After which cut was the piece shorter than 1 cm for the first time?
maths.answer: After cut 5. The piece was three quarters of a centimetre long.
maths.explain: Follow the line along the cuts. After cut 4, the piece was 1 and a half cm, which is longer than 1 cm. After cut 5, it was 0.75 cm, which is three quarters of a centimetre. That is the first one shorter than 1 cm.
maths.context: This is about the paper-cutting experiment. You cut a 24 cm strip in half again and again and measured each piece.

chart.title: Made-up example: how long the piece was after each cut
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what your results may look like. Each cut halves the piece. After 8 cuts it is about 1 millimetre long.

maths.why_maths: A line graph shows the whole experiment at once. Reading it tells you exactly when the pieces became too small to measure easily.

maths.problem: Imagine you cut EVERY piece in half each time, not just one. You start with 1 strip. After 1 cut you have 2 pieces, after 2 cuts you have 4. How many pieces after 5 cuts? After 10?
maths.answer: 32 pieces after 5 cuts, and 1,024 pieces after 10 cuts.
maths.explain: Each cut doubles the number of pieces: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. So 5 cuts make 32 pieces. Keep doubling: 64, 128, 256, 512, 1,024. So 10 cuts make 1,024 pieces. This doubling is why halving shrinks things so fast.
maths.context: This is about the paper-cutting experiment, where each cut halves the paper.

answer_chart.title: Cutting every piece in half each time

maths.why_maths: Halving and doubling are partners. Spotting the doubling pattern shows why only about 31 halvings take a strip all the way down to the width of an atom.

maths.problem: In the marble test with a battery hidden, you rolled 20 marbles. 18 went straight through and 1 turned aside. How many came back? In the real experiment, about 1 in 8,000 came back. Which was emptier: your card or the gold?
maths.answer: 1 marble came back. The gold was far emptier.
maths.explain: 18 + 1 = 19, and 20 - 19 = 1. So 1 marble came back. That is 1 in 20. In the real experiment, only 1 in 8,000 came back. 8,000 is 400 times bigger than 20. So the gold atoms' centres were a much smaller target, and the gold was far emptier than your card.
maths.context: This is about the marble test. You roll marbles under a card with something hidden under it, and count where they come out.

chart.title: Made-up example: what happened to 20 marbles when one battery was hidden

maths.why_maths: Counting what comes back, out of how many were rolled, is exactly how scientists measured the emptiness of atoms.

maths.problem: In the pencil-dot activity, you made 50 dots. 24 landed in the inner ring and 17 in the middle ring. How many landed in the outer ring? Draw a bar chart of the three rings.
maths.answer: 9 dots landed in the outer ring. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: 24 + 17 = 41. Then 50 - 41 = 9. So 9 dots landed in the outer ring. On the bar chart, the inner ring has the tallest bar, so most dots landed near the target.
maths.context: This is about the pencil-dot activity, where you close your eyes and dot at a target 50 times, then count the dots in rings.

answer_chart.title: Made-up example: where 50 pencil dots landed
answer_chart.note: The inner ring is also the smallest ring. So the dots are packed most tightly near the target.

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance where the dots are thickest. That is how scientists picture where an electron is most likely to be found.

maths.problem: One grain of salt holds about a million million million atoms. That is 1 followed by 18 zeros. If you counted one atom every second, without stopping, a year would let you count about 30 million. How many years would one grain take?
maths.answer: About 30 thousand million years. That is more than twice the age of the universe.
maths.explain: A million million million is 1,000,000,000,000,000,000. Dividing it by about 30 million a year gives about 30,000,000,000 years, which is 30 thousand million. The universe is about 14 thousand million years old. So counting the atoms in one grain of salt would take more than twice as long as the universe has existed.
maths.context: In the Dots Make Pictures activity, you looked at grains of salt through a magnifier. They are tiny cubes. Each one is a stack of atoms.
maths.why_maths: Atoms are so small that only very big numbers can count them. Comparing with seconds and years turns a number too big to imagine into something you can feel.
