how_we_found_out.context: How did scientists become sure that atoms are real, when nobody could see one? This card tells how people found out.
how_we_found_out.who: Robert Brown, a Scottish botanist, Albert Einstein, a German-born physicist, and Jean Perrin, a French physicist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Atoms are not real. They are only a handy way of thinking about chemistry.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1827, Robert Brown, a Scottish botanist, looked at pollen grains in water under a microscope. Tiny specks from inside the grains jiggled about and never stopped. At first he wondered if they were alive. Then he saw specks of crushed glass and rock jiggle in the same way. Nobody could explain it. By 1900, many chemists used atoms to explain how elements join. But some famous scientists, such as Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, said atoms were not real. Nobody had seen one, so they called atoms only a handy way of thinking. In 1905, Albert Einstein worked out what would happen if water really were made of moving molecules. Each speck would be bumped a little more on one side than the other, again and again, so it would jiggle. His maths said how far a speck should wander in a given time. In 1908, Jean Perrin in Paris watched specks under a microscope and measured how far they moved. The numbers matched Einstein's maths. From them, Perrin even worked out how big molecules are. Ostwald changed his mind and accepted that atoms are real. Perrin won the Nobel Prize in 1926.

roots.context: We have been learning that everything you can touch is made of atoms, and what atoms are made of. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Cut a strip of paper in half again and again, and each piece is still paper, for a while. After about 31 halvings, a piece would be only one atom wide. Its atoms are carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, the same kinds as in sugar and in you. None of them is paper, so if you cut anything far enough, the pieces are no longer that thing.
deep_truth.habit: We think a small piece of a thing is just a smaller copy of it, so a crumb of dosa is still dosa. That is true only down to a point. Below it, the pieces are atoms, and a carbon atom is not dosa or paper.
deep_truth.evidence: In the paper-cutting experiment, the last sliver was still paper, and the magnifier showed its plant fibres. The halving chart shows that a piece one atom wide is still about 23 halvings further down. Paper is mostly cellulose, which is built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Sugar is built from the same three kinds of atom.

three.who_am_i: You are made mostly of atoms of oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, the same kinds as in air and food. None of those atoms is 'you' by itself.
three.what_is_life: A living thing is built from the same kinds of atom as a stone or a star. Its atoms keep coming and going as it eats and breathes, yet it stays itself.
three.what_is_this_world: In this world, about 90 kinds of atom make everything you can touch. All of them are built from just three kinds of particle.

roots.thread: About 90 kinds of atom build everything you can touch. Each atom is built from only three kinds of particle: protons, neutrons and electrons. The same few particles become stars, rivers, mangoes and you, joined in different ways. Consciousness runs through all of it, down to every particle. So a mind is not something that appears only when atoms build a brain.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a banyan fruit, then one of its tiny seeds. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing at all.' Uddalaka says that from this finest part, which you cannot see, the great banyan tree grows.
teachings.link: When you cut the paper smaller and smaller, the pieces soon became too small to see. Yet everything big is built from far smaller particles, which nobody can see with their eyes.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at the hub of a wheel. It is the empty hole in the middle that makes the wheel useful. A pot is shaped from clay, but it is the empty space inside that holds things.
teachings.link: An atom is almost all empty space, and that space gives the atom its size. Because the electrons spread out around the nucleus, atoms take up room, so the things built from them do too.

science.text: Everything we can touch is made of about 90 kinds of atom, and every atom is built from protons, neutrons and electrons.

What an electron is doing between measurements is still argued about. Quantum physics does not prove that a person watching makes the world real. In physics, an 'observer' means anything that measures, such as a detector.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school in ancient India, and most physicists and brain scientists today
other_view.view: Only matter is real. Particles follow the rules of physics, but they have no experience of their own. Awareness appears only when matter is built into a living brain. Many careful thinkers hold this view.
